designed to rapidly generate comprehensive $N$-body simulations for modified gravity (MG) frameworks. This work details the code's implementation, validates it through numerical tests, and presents initial findings from an extensive suite of cosmological simulations covering three categories of MG models featuring conformal coupling: $f(R)$ gravity, symmetron, and coupled quintessence. Built upon the parallel particle-mesh framework GLAM, MG-GLAM utilizes an efficient multigrid relaxation method to resolve the characteristic nonlinear partial differential equations inherent to these models. Specifically for $f(R)$ gravity, we have integrated novel variants to expand model diversity and optimized the relaxation algorithms to ensure sustained computational performance. While this paper focuses on conformal coupling, a companion study addresses derivative coupling MG models, such as Vainshtein and K-mouflage types. MG-GLAM serves as a versatile and broad platform capable of modeling prototypes for most significant MG theories. The code is highly optimized, achieving a speedup exceeding one hundred times that of previous $N$-body codes while maintaining high accuracy in predicting the matter power spectrum and dark matter halo abundance. Consequently, MG-GLAM is exceptionally well-suited for producing large volumes of MG simulations required for constructing mock galaxy catalogues and generating precise emulators for current and upcoming galaxy surveys. MG-GLAM is now available for public download.

Since its release in 2012 with the GADGET code by Springel, $N$-body simulations have been a primary method for investigating the non-linear evolution and clustering of matter across various cosmological models. These simulations have been extensively employed to examine the physical properties of astrophysical objects, including galaxy and halo populations, as well as the characteristics of observable tracers like stars and quasars. Concurrently, emulator development has been utilized to maximize the output of high-resolution simulations. However, the escalating demands of modern and future galaxy survey projects, such as DES, Euclid, and LSST, require both the computational capacity to run massive simulation volumes and the creation of accurate emulators to enable statistical exploration of the vast parameter space of modified gravity (MG) models. Although previous efforts have made progress, existing codes and strategies have limitations that hinder these goals. This study evaluates the performance of four $N$-body simulation codes across a range of MG models to identify efficient computational methods and facilitate the development of a new code, MG-GLAM. This new tool rapidly solves prominent MG models by directly computing their underlying partial differential equations (PDEs).

equivalence class of pairs consisting of simply connected proper subdomains of $\mathbb{C}$ and Gaussian free fields (GFFs) defined on them, modulo conformal equivalence, specifically considering conformal mappings that fix $\infty$. In this work, we introduce the concept of conformal equivalence with respect to $\mathbb{C}$ by removing the condition that the conformal map must fix $\infty$. We demonstrate that this relaxed condition yields a broader class of equivalences, which we term near-conformal equivalences. Furthermore, we establish the existence of GFFs on domains obtained by applying near-conformal maps to the underlying domains of GFFs that match their covariances locally. Finally, we provide upper and lower bound estimates for the differences between the real and imaginary parts of the GFF on these near-conformal domains. These findings are potentially significant for analyzing the covariance structure of the GFF across complex geometries, such as Riemann surfaces with and without boundaries, as well as for estimating the regularity of the inverse Laplacian with Dirichlet boundary conditions on such surfaces. Numerical simulations confirm the validity of our main results. Additionally, proofs of all lemmas and propositions are included in the appendix to streamline the main text.

Wiki platform that transforms wikis into robust environments for collaborating on publication-ready manuscripts and software initiatives. Created within Jonathan Dushoff's theoretical biology lab at McMaster University, it enables users to jointly tackle any task achievable through UNIX commands that convert textual "source code" into final outputs. Researchers can utilize it to collaborate on programs in languages such as R, Python, C, or others, alongside specialized features designed to streamline LaTeX document creation. This tool leverages the wiki medium to function simultaneously as a collaborative text editor, development environment, version control system, and publishing platform. Its applications are highly adaptable; its processing is governed by customizable makefiles, and its modular architecture is built to facilitate adaptation for various other uses. The platform's flexibility and robustness stem from its foundation on the versatile MediaWiki software and its integration with Makefiles and UNIX utilities. Its source code is available on GitHub, and while its primary design context is the Dushoff theory lab, it is entirely portable and can be implemented in any other setting. WW was developed by Jonathan Dushoff and Andrew McKellar. Its history, feature set, and customization options are detailed in the WW makefile, which every WW instance possesses, and these can be explored using the 'show WW' wiki command. WW emerged from versions created in 2010, 2011, and 2012, with its origins and evolution facilitated by NUPA (Now You Can Use PAW), another makefile-based collaborative platform also built on MediaWiki. WW can be obtained via its GitHub repository or by downloading the WW makefile from another wiki; in the latter case, users simply need to load the external makefile. WW operates within the simple wiki framework, utilizing a straightforward interface with a minimal set of built-in features, although it supports a complex "visual" interface via plugins like TWBootstrap and ModernTW (which must be separately installed and configured). WW relies on the Unmakefile module (available on GitHub) to execute any other makefile, and it incorporates the now obsolete WPMultiImage module for handling multiple images. Additionally, it utilizes the now obsolete WikiProcessingTeX extension for processing LaTeX files, though this can be replaced by loading an external makefile such as one derived from the now obsolete CollaborativeLaTeX (coLaTeX) project. WW employs the Make extension to generate interfaces analogous to UNIX makefiles, and it uses the Cite extension for its reference management system. -air jet flame to forecast how the reacting flow responds to upstream acoustic actuation. Within a linearized framework, capturing heat release fluctuations is essential for studying thermoacoustic instabilities and flame noise. Distinct from prior work, this study employs an active flame approach, which incorporates heat release oscillations induced by acoustic fluctuations. Implementing this approach linearly requires linearizing a combustion model; however, linearizing Large Eddy Simulation (LES) and Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) models creates closure issues, rendering them difficult to apply in this context. Conversely, Reynolds-averaged Navier Stokes (RANS) models effectively avoid these problems, making them ideal for this application. These RANS models were linearized around the time-averaged flow of the jet flame, with linear responses to small amplitude oscillations (approximately 1% of the mean velocity) calculated using resolvent analysis. This method identifies the most energetic response to any input forcing at specific frequencies and wavenumves. The computation of a linearized RANS model, which includes a linearized $k-\epsilon$ turbulence model and a finitenrate chemistry model, is detailed. This model accurately captures the dominant feedback loops responsible for jet flame noises, which were derived from non-linear simulations using a LES solver. Notably, the linear analysis correctly predicts the scalng of noise intensity with respect to turbulence. Furthermore, the research examines the feedback mechanisms underlying noises at two distinct frequencies: a near-field noise arising from the shear layer instability and a far-field noise generated by the acoustic resonance of the jet. Overall, this study demonstrates that linearized RANS models serve as a powerful tool for predicting fluctuations in reacting flows, even within highly turbulent flows, and for elucidating the feedback loops that cause reacting flows to oscillate.

If this interaction violates lepton number, the $\Delta L=2$ transition is directly mediated by the dark matter field, bypassing the suppression typically caused by small neutrino masses, thereby producing a significant effect on decay rates. Because ultralight dark matter behaves as a classical field, the resulting decay events exhibit a periodic modulation. However, we observe that in the early Universe, such a coupling would likely disrupt standard cosmological models. Specifically, the necessity for neutrinos to free-stream prior to matter-radiation equality imposes strict constraints on the parameter space, rendering the detection of any signal in future $0\nu \beta\beta$ experiments extremely unlikely, even with meV-level sensitivity to the effective neutrino mass. To achieve this, the mismatch between the two components of the dominant CP-even neutrino mass eigenstate must be precisely tuned to zero. We outline how this fine-tuning can arise naturally from neutrino oscillation data, potentially linked to the mass of a second, heavier seesaw gauge boson. This mechanism represents a specific instance of an oscillating dark matter scenario, which can be generalized to other fundamental fields, such as the dark photon. We elucidate the requisite conditions for this to occur within a Type-I seesaw framework featuring two heavy right-handed neutrinos, utilizing the geometric representation of neutrino masses to visualize the parameter space. This model can be probed not only through $0\nu \beta\beta$ decay but also via neutrino oscillations, the mass of the heavier right-handed neutrino, and the dark matter density. Furthermore, we extend this analysis to the case of majorana neutrinos mixing with sterile states. Ultimately, we establish that the inability to detect this signal in upcoming experiments would strongly imply either that neutrinos are dirac or that the neutrino mass is generated purely by the type-I seesaw mechanism. We conclude by discussing extensions involving dark matter scalar hair and magnetic moment interactions. Overall, we propose a concrete, testable scenario: we embed this simplest oscillating dark matter model into a Type-I seesaw with two heavy right-handed neutrinos, determining the necessary parameter values, and illustrating how different neutrino mass eigenstates can be investigated across various experimental and astrophysical contexts. Keyword: 14.60.Pq, 12.60.Fr, 12.60Th, 95.35.De,

, nonlocal extension of Einstein's gravitational theory, modeled after the analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics in media. Within this framework, historical dependence is introduced through a constitutive relation that utilizes a causal kernel, which must ultimately be derived from observational data. This paper aims to reformulate nonlocal gravity so that the nonlocal components of the constitutive relation directly link measurable quantities, mirroring the approach found in nonlocal electrodynamics. The derived constitutive relation aligns with a recent proposal by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl [25]. Utilizing this updated constitutive relation for NLG, it is demonstrated that de Sitter spacetime does not constitute a valid solution. Furthermore, when the underlying local theory is general relativity (GR), the constituent relation indicates that the actual constituent of GR is not dark energy but rather a material with extremely high stiffness and slowness. In the context of galaxy rotation curves within NLG, the constituent relation reveals three distinct components of dark matter: a component with near-vacuum characteristics, a component with high but finite elasticity, and a component exhibiting fluid-like behavior. These findings support the hypothesis that the components of dark matter and dark energy can be explained within NLG using a constitutive relation analogous to that of piezoelectric materials. Additionally, the governing integro-differential equations for galaxy rotation curves, which were previously proposed ad hoc, can now be recovered via this constitutive relation. Collectively, these results suggest that the constituent relations of certain dark components can be understood through the lens of nonlocal electrodynamics and nonlocal gravity, providing a straightforward constitutive model for these components. Consequently, the magnitude of the "dark sector" may be, at least in part, an artifact of the constitutive model of NLG. Ultimately, the general constitutive relation for NLG offers a promising pathway for developing constitutive models of dark matter and dark energy based on the well-established GR. General constitutive relations for NLG can also be applied to other gravitational models, such as $f(R)$ gravity, to elucidate their inherent constitutive mechanisms. To achieve this, however, the current constitutive relation must be supplemented with additional constitutive equations that define the specific historical dependencies. Until then, claims regarding the existence or absence of dark matter and dark energy within NLG may remain somewhat ad hoc. Keywords: nonlocal gravity, constitutive relation, dark matter, dark energy, galaxy rotation curves, de Sitter spacetime, causality, pie

We present a statistical framework that leverages genome-wide association statistics to pinpoint classes of genomic elements that are either enriched for or depleted regarding loci influencing a specific trait, with the model inherently accommodating multiple annotation types. Applying this approach to GWAS data for 18 human traits—including red and platelet cell metrics, glucose and lipid levels, height, BMI, and Crohn's disease—we assessed the relevance of 450 genomic annotations across over a hundred tissues and cell lines, covering protein-coding genes, enhancers, and DNase-I hypersensitive sites. Our results indicate that the proportion of phenotype-associated SNPs affecting protein sequences varies by trait, ranging from approximately 2% for platelet volume to roughly 20% for LDL cholesterol. Additionally, we observed significant depletion of repressed chromatin for SNPs linked to several traits and enrichment of cell type-specific DNase-I hypersensitive sites for others (e.g., spleen-specific sites for platelet volume). Finally, re-weighting GWAS results using functional genomics data increased the count of high-confidence associated loci by approximately 5%. However, other annotation combinations yielded fewer loci or no improvement over using genome-wide padding, underscoring the challenge of translating genomic hits into precise molecular mechanisms. Overall, our methodology offers a conservative yet practical way to integrate functional genomics annotations for prioritizing GWAS findings. The R code is available at http://www.genestudies.org/functional-enrichment/.

Genomic sequencing now readily identifies rare variants, yet determining their functional impact is often challenging. By combining population HapMap phase 2 data with a prediction of rare variant effects, we show that rare variants contribute substantially to the heritability of coronary artery disease (CAD), a finding robust to assumptions about frequency-dependent selection. Although rare variants explain roughly half of the CAD heritability, they account for only about 5% of genome-wide significant SNPs, suggesting many associated variants have moderate effects. These variants are enriched in regulatory regions near protein-coding genes, a pattern that aligns well with the observed over-representation of rare variants causing loss of function in such regions. We advocate for using genomic functional enrichment to guide the prioritization of rare variants and other GWAS findings.

Galactic Centre that have not exhibited outbursts over a ten-year monitoring period has led to the hypothesis of a substantial population of stellar-mass black holes in this area. A fundamental premise of this argument is the assertion that neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) do not experience long intervals between transients. However, this paper demonstrates that approximately half of the known transient LMXBs with confirmed neutron star primaries exhibit recurrence times exceeding a decade when observed with MAXI sensitivity. Furthermore, we show that to align the expected total number of neutron star LMXBs with both current observations and the galaxy's millisecond radio pulsar population, the dominant class of these systems must have recurrence times far surpassing a century for MAXI-detectable outbursts, implying that few such systems have been identified to date. We argue that the primary objective in coming years should be the detection of neutron star LMXBs via precise astrometric measurements using the Gaia mission. By exploiting the full range of masses among these binaries, the Gaia-based estimates for the total population are significantly lower than those derived from X-rays alone, thereby reducing the inferred total number of stellar-mass black holes in the Galactic Centre from the disputed lower limit of ~20,000 to a value only marginally greater than the well-documented stellar count in that region.

Mirroring classical Coriolis and centrifugal forces, these phenomena include spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, centrifugal spin-orbit coupling, and centrifugal redshift. The duration of these effects, which can persist for several picoseconds following excitation, depends on phonon decay rates. Terahertz laser control of chemical reactions, beyond simply increasing reactivity, may enable the creation of reactive species that are otherwise unstable or inaccessible. Since its introduction in 1947, semiconductor $p-n$ junctions have been central to modern electronics. However, these traditional devices are now approaching their physical limitations in terms of speed, size, and energy efficiency. To address these constraints, there is growing interest in $p-n$ homojunctions utilizing heavy-hole or light-hole valence bands, composed of materials with distinct properties. This perspective article examines recent advancements in these emerging homogeneous $p-n$ junctions, detailing how differences in effective mass, spin-orbit coupling, and lattice constants across the interface give rise to physically distinct phenomena. These include centrifugal barriers, quantum centrifugal fountains, enhanced tunneling effects, and modified Kondo interactions. By comparing traditional and homogeneous $p-n$ junctions, we emphasize the novel physical mechanisms at play in these systems and suggest potential applications in novel device designs, including centrifugal barriers, fountain diodes, and enhanced Kondo switch diodes.

First, we introduce a new metric leveraging Natural Language Inference (NLI) to assess the semantic variety of a model's response set. Validated against an existing framework (Tevet and Berant, 2021), our findings strongly suggest that NLI Diversity aligns with semantic diversity; notably, the contradiction relation proves more effective than the neutral relation for this purpose, and integrating the NLI model's confidence yields state-of-the-art performance. Second, we present an iterative generation method termed Diversity Threshold Generation, which significantly boosts the semantic diversity of sampled responses, achieving an average 137% increase in NLI Diversity over standard generation techniques. This approach ensures that generated texts span a wider range of semantics, as confirmed by both NLI Diversity and human evaluations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this enhanced diversity positively impacts the overall quality of diverse responses, as measured by human-assessed metrics. Iterative generation with a diversity-focused threshold not only maximizes semantic diversity but also preserves coherence and fluency. We release all our findings, including human evaluation data, to aid future research. Our experiments indicate that this method generalizes across various dialogue lengths, models, and domains. Like Tevet and Berant (2021), we utilize HuggingFace transformers for evaluation and generation. We document the increase in semantic diversity of generated texts using NLI Diversity Threshold Generation compared to baseline methods. Additionally, we provide detailed analyses of confidence settings, PR curves, the impact of batch sizes, multi-label NLI scenarios, and the generalizability of NLI-based diversity metrics beyond multi-class classification. We also explore the balance between quality and diversity in diverse generation and analyze the semantic spaces of different classifiers. We have numerically modeled these rotating objects to determine whether they can sustain nuclear fusion as their energy source, accounting for significant rotational deformation rather than assuming slow rotation. For various angular momentum values, we derived critical curves in the mass versus central degeneracy parameter space where nuclear energy generation equals surface luminosity. Our results indicate that when angular momentum surpasses a threshold of $J_0=8.85\times 10^{48}{\rm erg}~{\rm s}$, the critical curve splits into two branches representing lower and higher degeneracy due to the mass-shedding limit. Based on these findings, we simulated the mechano-thermal evolution of substellar objects under two simplified scenarios involving cooling and reductions in mass or angular momentum. In the first scenario, dominated by external braking mechanisms like magnetized winds or magnetic braking, the evolution is primarily governed by the spin-down timescale. In the second scenario, lacking external braking, gravitational contraction drives the object to the mass-shedding limit, after which it ejects mass to form a surrounding ring or disc and subsequently shrinks. These simulations occur prior to any hydrogen shell burning ignition. Our findings demonstrate that both scenarios can result in objects around $0.12 M_\odot$ acquiring significant spin, causing them to shed mass and create a ring or disc at roughly $8.2{\rm } R_\odot$ post-ignition. These outcomes align with the observed properties of classical cataclysmic variables and accretion disc-transiting planetary objects. Ultimately, this study provides a foundational understanding of the evolution, braking, and mass shedding in low-mass stars hosting planetary systems.

These structures are frequently depicted in a two-tiered layout, where each entity set is shown as a collection of vertices aligned on one of two parallel horizontal lines, and their relationships are illustrated by edges linking corresponding vertices across the lines. A primary goal in creating such visualizations is to reduce edge crossings; however, minimizing crossings is computationally demanding and often yields drawings with so many intersections that they compromise readability. This work examines a recent method for eliminating crossings by splitting vertices, aiming to identify the minimum number of vertices that must be split to achieve a planar representation. We demonstrate that deciding whether a planar drawing is achievable by splitting at most $k$ vertices is fixed parameter tractable with respect to $k$. Furthermore, we show that this problem admits a 2-$apxPTAS$. In contrast, for general graphs, we prove that any algorithm that plansarizes a drawing by splitting vertices using few $O(1)$-splittable crossings requires at least $\Omega(\sqrt{\log \log n})$ crossings, where $n$ is the input size. Additionally, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(n^{2/3})$ for the problem of minimizing split vertices to planarize a drawing. These findings extend prior research by Krawczyk et al. for thruster-assisted bipedal robot walking. Assuming well-tuned supervisory controllers, we concentrate on refining desired joint trajectories to meet specific performance goals. To ensure these constraints are met, we develop an intermediary filter grounded in reference governors. Since modifications and impact events cause deviations from desired periodic orbits, we robustly guarantee hybrid invariance by employing a predictive scheme within a bounded time framework. Because the resulting hybrid optimization problem operates under conditions of high nonlinearity and dimension, we enhance computational efficiency by transforming it into a Quadratic Program (QP). Regarding gait generation, we adopt a recently introduced hybrid Poincaré map control strategy that significantly reduces problem complexity. While this map-based approach typically requires only model prediction, we utilize the map instead of a traditional Zeno-based scheme to trigger impacts. This integration allows for the straightforward achievement of constrained performance, such as maintaining constant or oscillating forward velocities, adapting to perturbations, and reacting to time-critical events. Although the map reduces the dimensional complexity of the intermediary scheme, it was recently shown that this still lacks the efficiency of direct gait generation methods. Consequently, we introduce a reconstruction algorithm for the map-based scheme and demonstrate that applying this algorithm to the intermediary controller yields a direct gait generation map that retains the constraints and robustness of the original hybrid Poincaré map control while offering superior computational efficiency. Simulation results validate the proposed approach, showcasing both the performance and, in the case of the direct map, the performance-bound guarantees of the proposed schemes. Furthermore, these findings illustrate how the intermediate filter enables the straightforward addition of constrained performance to the modern bimanual robot gait generation literature. Although developed for bipedal robots, this methodology is broadly applicable to any dynamical system capable of gaiting.

Beyond this new technique, we identify a previously unrecognized source of slowdown by analyzing cache eviction as a root cause. The resulting performance degradation is substantially greater than previous methods, thereby enhancing the time granularity available for Flush+Reload attacks. We evaluated HyperDegrade across various Intel microarchitectures, achieving significant slowdowns that, in specific microbenchmark scenarios, represent a three-order-of-magnitude improvement over state-of-the-art solutions. To assess the effectiveness of performance degradation in amplifying side channels, we introduced and validated specific leakage metrics. Our findings indicate that HyperDegrade improves time granularity without compromising trace quality. Furthermore, we conducted a fair comparison of three performance degradation strategies when paired with Flush+Reload from an attacker's viewpoint. We also devised an attack targeting an underutilized vulnerability in OpenSSL, where HyperDegrade demonstrated superior efficacy by reducing the number of required Flush+Reload traces needed for success by a factor of three. In terms of cryptographic contributions, we revisited the recently proposed Raccoon attack on TLS-DH key exchanges, extending its application to other protocols. Leveraging HyperDegrade, we constructed an end-to-end attack proving that Raccoon-like exploits can succeed with real data, addressing a gap left by earlier research. Utilizing this approach, we achieved a significant breakthrough by demonstrating that the shared secret in DSA key exchanges can be extracted with approximately 1.5× the sorting table size, overcoming the former limitation of needing a size exceeding half of the sorting table. This was accomplished by effectively applying the BGGW optimization to attack traces. Our results confirm that HyperDegrade attack traces meet the rigorous criteria for successfully executing the BGGW optimization on real data. By combining these attacks, we highlight the necessity of updating the size constraints for feasible Raccoon and related strategies. Additionally, we showed how to apply this approach to Feistel ciphers, extending the maximum size of a feasible Raccoon-like attack from 50% to 75% of the key size for 32-byte keys, or precisely solving the key extraction problem for keys exceeding 50% of the block size. We achieved this by utilizing the full potential of performance degradation in an "inside attack," contrasting with the "outside attack" demonstrated with HyperDegrade. to knot diagrams. It is possible to convert any knot diagram into a trivial unknot diagram through a combination of unknotting operations and Reidemeister moves. These operations hold substantial significance in knot theory, particularly for analyzing knot complexity and invariants. Furthermore, they play a crucial role in fields such as biology, chemistry, and physics, where they help investigate the complex entanglements found in strings, organic molecules, and DNA. This paper introduces a novel unknotting operation known as the diagonal move, applicable to both classical and welded knots. We demonstrate that the crossing change, Delta-move, Sharp-move, Gamma-move, n-gon move, pass move, and 4-move can all be achieved via sequences of diagonal moves. Additionally, we define a distance metric based on the diagonal move and examine its characteristics. These distances are determined using a corresponding algebraic invariant called the negative plactic algebra. We also establish bounds for these bounds and compare our findings with distances derived from other invariants, specifically the Jones polynomial and the Homfly polynomial. An accompanying online resource is available at https://www.researchgate.net/publication/367974001_The_Diagonal_Move_and_Its_Applications, which contains an implementation of the diagonal move algorithm in C++ and provides examples of knots with minimal diagonal distances. The code is written to be accessible to individuals without knot theory expertise, who can utilize it to compute the distance between two knots using the diagonal move. **Keywords:** Diagonal move, Welded knot, Plactic order, Plactic monoid, Plactic algebra, Negative plactic algebra, Jones polynomial, Homfly polynomial, 4-move, n-gon move, Pass move, Delta-move, Sharp-move, Gamma-move, n-gon move, Knot complexity, Invariants, Entanglement. **AMS Subject Classification:** 57M25, 57M27, 57M25, 58J50, 58N15.

Multi-agent collaboration is increasingly essential for addressing complex challenges across various fields. However, developing effective joint behaviors among a vast number of diverse agents remains a significant obstacle. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework for training large swarms of simple agents by exploiting the cyclic spectral features of a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN). This approach, which we term Searchspace-GAN, offers an efficient and effective method for encoding complex multi-agent search behaviors within a low-dimensional manifold. By leveraging the compactness of this representation, our required data for training remains consistently small, even when scaling to swarms containing thousands of agents. Experimental results on a robotic arm manipulation task show that we can utilize just 512 training samples to train a swarm of 20 agents and only 1,024 samples for a swarm of 100 agents. By utilizing this low-dimensional search space, we employ gradient descent to optimize a network predicting the coefficients used to combine basis behaviors to perform a new task. Since GANs are differentiable, this process allows us to directly and efficiently train the task predictor network. By searching for tasks within this low-dimensional space, we transform the difficult problem of jointly training many agents into a scalable solution where the search complexity depends solely on the dimensionality of the search space, independent of the swarm size. On the Cheetah dataset, we demonstrate that searchspace-GAN is 10x more sample-efficient than current state-of-the-art methods and yields a scalable collaborative robot system requiring 50x fewer samples. Additionally, we introduce a new insight into multi-agent search behaviors, revealing that they can be represented via a "respiratory pattern" within a low-dimensional manifold.-novel-task-nash-equilibrium

Based on whether participation is mandatory or optional, FL can be structured as either conventional or robust federated learning. However, existing research has focused predominantly on conventional frameworks, often overlooking the practical challenges inherent in robust settings. A primary obstacle in such systems is communication overhead, a critical bottleneck in large-scale distributed environments. To mitigate this, this work investigates the application of model compression techniques to FL, specifically exploring a novel and difficult scenario where a power law distribution of data overtraining occurs among high-volume contributors in robust federated learning. This distribution causes a disproportionate training investment in a few power users, leading to overtraining effects that adversely impact the overall model quality. We developed a theoretical model to demonstrate that this distribution is a key driver of overtraining in both conventional and robust FL. Furthermore, we created a communication-efficient, distributed model compression scheme tailored for this power law distribution. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to address communication-intensive model compression in a robust federated learning context. Through extensive simulations, we validated that our method outperforms both traditional model compression approaches and other existing compression schemes across various real-world datasets. By outlining a clear roadmap for future opportunities, this work provides a comprehensive analysis of communication-efficient model compression in federated learning environments.

To overcome this, Random Fourier Features (RFF) were introduced to approximate kernel functions using randomized Fourier features, enabling scalability. Despite its popularity, RFF has notable limitations: because it samples features from a distribution independent of the training data, it demands a large number of feature dimensions to match the performance of kernelized classifiers, a requirement that scales with dataset size. Consequently, reducing feature dimensions is essential for effective scaling. This paper introduces Pseudo Random Fourier Features (PRFF), a data-dependent kernel approximation technique designed to minimize feature dimensions and enhance predictive performance. The method is evaluated on classification and regression tasks, with comparisons made against RFF, orthogonal random features, and the Nyström approach. PRFF demonstrates superior performance across both tasks and is particularly efficient at high dataset volumes, requiring only 20% of the feature dimensions that RFF needs. Furthermore, the study provides analytical insights into the underlying mechanisms of both PRFF and RFF. Experimental results confirm that PRFF is easy to implement and scalable, maintaining a constant dimension requirement regardless of dataset size. PRFF achieves a 5x reduction in dimensionality compared to RFF while maintaining performance within 2% of the Gaussian kernel, and it processes 10x more data points per second. Overall, PRFF is highly competitive with other linearized kernel approaches, exhibits the fastest training and prediction speeds, and is exceptionally accurate at low dimensionality levels. The source code is available at https://github.com/hosseinalizadeh/PRFF.

Traditional methods for assessing attack effectiveness typically rely on macro-level metrics, like the critical percolation probability ($p_c$) and the size of the giant component, often overlooking the micro-level dynamics of node removals, their specific traits, and immediate outcomes. This paper introduces and applies a micro-scale approach to attack analysis. Grounded in network percolation theory, we examine the "avalanche" effect triggered by the removal of a single node from the giant component—a phenomenon where one removal causes a cascade of disconnections that significantly contributes to network fragmentation and immunization beyond the loss of that single node. We specifically analyze the avalanche size, defined as the count of nodes disconnected from the giant component due to one removal. Through simulation-based analysis of random attacks on scale-free networks, we demonstrate that random removals generate non-trivial avalanches with events exceeding the $p_c$ threshold capable of immunizing the network. Furthermore, we reveal that the critical exponent characterizing avalanche size distribution near $p_c$ aligns with that of earthquake size distribution, suggesting these events may be analyzed using the same theoretical framework. These findings indicate that random network attacks function similarly to scale-invariant processes, offering a novel perspective on random attack dynamics and their link to network immunization. The proposed concepts and discovery methods can be utilized to characterize random attacks across various complex systems, such as social and technical networks. Additionally, since non-random attacks typically induce larger avalanches than random ones, understanding avalanche mechanisms in random attacks aids in developing effective strategies against targeted attacks. Finally, we propose that random attacks follow a selforganized process to maximize avalanche size without causing network collapse.

While previous research has examined over-parameterized linear models with non-sparse, high-dimensional data, those findings largely rely on the assumption of independent samples. This study investigates linear regression under over-parameterization with dependent time series data. We propose an interpolation-based estimator and establish a theoretical framework for its excess risk across various dependence structures. This approach accommodates infinite-dimensional data without requiring sparsity and unifies the handling of long-memory processes. Furthermore, we bound the risk using integrated covariance and the nondegeneracy of autocorrelation matrices. Although this phenomenon is often blamed on forecasting inaccuracies or operational breakdowns, we argue it stems from risk-averse scheduling strategies. By applying a stochastic self-scheduling model to real-world data from the Australian National Electricity Market, we show that risk-averse storage units adopt a short-sighted operational approach. Specifically, they focus primarily on near-term price arbitrage, targeting only a limited number of extreme price peaks and valleys, which leaves them inactive during many periods characterized by significantly high or low prices. These findings carry significant policy weight, particularly given the lack of transparency surrounding unit-level risk aversion and the visible risks involved in intervention decisions. Consequently, regulators should consider laboratory-based testing environments, such as the Digital Twin of the National Electricity Market, to enhance understanding of storage behavior and refine market design policies.

The model incorporates simplified linear boundary layer friction, Newtonian cooling, and dry convective adjustment. Numerical experiments were conducted to examine how varying the global horizontal advection strength influences the development of zonal mean circulation cells in response to thermal wind balance. These results were subsequently integrated into a comprehensive GCM that includes nonlinear features such as area-integrated convection and cloud radiative forcing. The study reveals three distinct regimes for circulation cell strength based on horizontal advection intensity: a friction-dominated regime with weak advection, an adjustment regime with intermediate advection, and an radiative-convective adjustment regime with strong advection. Radiative-convective equilibrium was determined by balancing large-scale convection with radiative energy fluxes, marking it as the atmosphere's intrinsic state in the absence of frictional dissipation. These regime boundaries were analyzed across planetary conditions ranging from Mars- to Venus-like. Furthermore, the impact of convective closure schemes on the radiative-convective equilibrium was explored, with findings indicating that these schemes can generate multiple equilibrium states, potentially leading to hysteresis and regime shifts on Venus and worlds with thicker atmospheres. Finally, the predicted regime characteristics were compared against the real Martian atmosphere, and it was concluded that the present Mars operates within the friction-dominated regime, likely due to its tenuous atmosphere and low convective efficiency. The proposed simplified GCM framework, particularly its parameterization of horizontal advection, can serve as a tool for exploring how changes in planetary friction, rotation, obliquity, and stellar or radiative-convective boundary conditions influence the complexity of global circulation, including the emergence of zonal jets, on Venus, Earth, and exoplanets. AL is particularly valuable in large-scale industrial applications where labeling expenses are high, prompting practitioners to utilize every available technique to enhance model accuracy. The recent achievements of self-supervised pretraining (SSP) underscore the significance of leveraging vast amounts of unlabeled data to improve model outcomes. In this study, we investigate the combination of AL and SSP using ImageNet. We observe that performance on small toy datasets—the standard benchmark in current literature—does not accurately reflect performance on ImageNet, as active learners tend to select easy samples. Drawing inspiration from this, we introduce a label augmentation technique to address this issue. With label augmentation, the outcomes on ImageNet differ markedly from those on toy datasets; specifically, AL surpasses random sampling only when sampled from a distribution centered on hard, misclassified images in a DNN classifier trained on the selected samples. Similar findings hold true for a larger low-cost label augmentation strategy, which can be readily implemented even within simple AL frameworks.

Our analysis reveals that the label distribution used during training is more critical than the mechanism for choosing instances to be labeled. We propose using a label distribution that assigns higher probability to hard, misleading, or out-of-distribution samples, noting that emphasizing any single category of difficult samples yields inferior results compared to a balanced approach. Although we focus on AL over self-supervised pretraining, these conclusions are broadly applicable. We conclude that, much like the label distribution, the choice of optimization hyperparameters and the order of algorithmic steps significantly impact the final performance.

Formulating DP for graphs is challenging due to the difficulty in defining meaningful neighbor relations across different graph objects. Consequently, various private learning algorithms on graphs have been developed that employ DP based on distinct differential definitions. Consequently, there is an urgent need for a rigorous and formal framework to define DP on graph data. This line of work is contingent upon defining appropriate differential privacy guarantees on graphs, a task that remains challenging. Using this framework as a foundation, we analyze current DP algorithms on graphs and demonstrate that many widely used methods on social network data lack true differential privacy guarantees. Finally, we offer suggestions for developing new DP algorithms within a unified framework. In this study, we develop a novel stochastic hydrodynamic method within the positive-P phase-space framework specifically for interacting Bose gases. This approach surpasses current hydrodynamic models, including superfluid and generalized hydrodynamics, by enabling the simulation of complete quantum dynamics; it can calculate non-equilibrium quantum correlations, even at short wavelengths. Based on this framework, we formulate a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme that extends the simulation duration for non-equilibrium scenarios beyond the limits of the full positive-P method, though this involves approximating quantum fluctuations. We demonstrate that this linearized scheme aligns directly with established Bogoliubov methods. Additionally, we validate the utility and benefits of this formalism by investigating correlations in a quantum shock wave scenario and contrasting its predictions with other standard quantum many-body approaches. Although developed for bosonic systems, this formalism is broadly applicable to any quantum system possessing a particle number conservation law.

Quantum hydrodynamics offers a potent framework for analyzing strongly interacting quantum many-body systems that drive complex phenomena in diverse systems, from cold atoms to quark-gluon plasmas. This "quantum fluid" concept relies on precise definitions of quantum pressure and viscosity, or viscosity-like viscoelasticity, which are inherently difficult to determine. We demonstrate that these properties can be accurately calculated using a recent stochastic method we term the LSW method (Leggett-Stormer-Weldon). This method draws inspiration from the time-evolution of stochastic potentials in the PEP path-integral formulation, extending the Feynman path integral to complex time. We validate the method's correctness and superiority by comparing it with standard quantum mechanics in simulations of expansion from quantum quenches in 1D and 2D. The LSW method represents a significant advancement over the SSW method (Stormer-Weldon-Weiss), which applies to systems with broken U(1) symmetry; together, these methods constitute a cutting-edge suite of tools for exploring the intricate dynamics of quantum many-body systems. The LSW and SSW methods are straightforward to implement in various scenarios and can be utilized to examine the post-collision phase of strongly interacting quantum gases, a critical aspect of modeling quark-gluon plasmas in heavy-ion collisions. Furthermore, these methods are general and can be employed to solve the time-dependent Schrödinger equation for any quantum system.

In the context of the annealed large deviation principle (LDP) for the empirical process of these words, the rate function corresponds to the specific relative entropy between the observed and reference laws of words. Birkner, Greven, and den Hollander \cite{BGdH10} established the quenched LDP (conditional on a typical letter sequence) for scenarios where renewal times exhibit an algebraic tail; their derived rate function consists of two components: the annealed rate function and a second term proportional to the specific relative entropy between the observed and reference laws of letters, where the reference law is generated by concatenating words and randomizing the origin. This proportionality constant matches the tail exponent of the renewal process. The current paper aims to generalize both LDPs to cases where the underlying letter sequences are not i.i.d. It demonstrates that both principles remain valid when the letter sequence satisfies a mixing condition known as \emph{summable variation}. The resulting rate functions are still expressed as specific relative entropies with respect to the reference laws of words and letters, respectively. However, because neither reference law is i.i.d., the extension requires several approximation arguments. A key component of this work is a novel decomposition of the relative entropy between two stationary processes, which may have independent applications. When the renewal times are not independent but form a Markov chain—specifically a Doeblin chain—the LDPs for empirical processes follow directly from the corresponding properties of the empirical distribution of states. Throughout the study, estimates of relative entropies between Markov chains play a central role.

used technique for evaluating machine learning models, facilitating both model selection and parameter optimization. However, because CV relies on random data partitioning, the resulting performance estimates are stochastic and can exhibit significant variability, particularly in natural language processing (NLP). We show that such unstable estimates are unsuitable for effective parameter tuning; consequently, the selected parameters are highly sensitive to data splits, often leading to sub-optimal choices and severe reproducibility challenges.

To address this, we propose employing J-K-fold CV, which utilizes J independent K-fold cross-validations to assess performance. Our primary contributions involve extending J-K-fold CV to the domain of parameter tuning and exploring strategies for selecting optimal values for J and K. We argue that minimizing variability is more critical than reducing bias for successful tuning, advocating for lower-than-typical values of K in NLP literature. This allows computational resources to be redirected toward increasing J. To validate the broad applicability of our recommendations, we examine a diverse set of case studies, including sentiment classification (both general and target-specific), part-of-speech tagging, and document classification. Our findings offer practical, evidence-based guidance for setting J and K across various tasks. Specifically, we recommend utilizing approximately 80% of one's computational budget for J and reserving 20% for parameter tuning when employing 5 independent 5-fold CV runs.

Momentum transfer from light to atoms causes a Doppler shift in the absorption spectrum, which only appears when the natural linewidth exceeds the Doppler width, which scales with detector momentum uncertainty. The standard absorption equation must be updated to include both the Doppler and photon recoil terms; failing to account for recoil introduces significant errors in high-precision momentum measurements. Our analysis yields a direct measurement of the photon recoil frequency for the lithium atom: $\hbar \mathbf{k}_{6472}\mathbf{c}^{-1} = 1.5087119(63)$ a.u., which demonstrates excellent agreement with the most precise previous determinations using photon spectroscopy. Furthermore, we provide parametric estimates of this recoil frequency for the four other resonance lines of neutral lithium, based on the most accurate existing data. These estimates gain significant precision following our direct measurement, with an expected uncertainty of $3 \times 10^{-7}$. To our knowledge, this represents the first such estimates for other resonance lines in any atom. We also present equation (6), which offers a general method for making high-precision estimates of photon recoil frequencies for other resonances given a direct measurement of one. Equations (3) and (4) quantify the small discrepancies between the standard and corrected absorption laws, while figure 4 illustrates why the standard law becomes inaccurate near the resonance frequency when the natural linewidth is large compared to the Doppler width. Additionally, table 1 summarizes all estimates and measurements of photon recoil frequencies for lithium's resonances, and we confirm that the minimum uncertainty in these values corresponds to approximately one absorbed photon.

a free-breathing, respiratory motion-compensated 4D (3D plus respiration) $T_2$-weighted turbo spin echo sequence suitable for radiology and MR-guided radiotherapy applications.

**Approach:** Continuous k-space data were collected using a rewound Cartesian acquisition with spiral ordering. This method was paired with a non-rigid grid registration analysis (NRGA). To ensure optimal image quality and efficient 4D coverage, NRGA was implemented within an asymmetric, reduced field-of-view, highly parallel, and compressed sensing framework. This setup utilized a time-of-flight encoding for the phase-encode direction. Additionally, an optimized variable flip angle scheme was employed to extend the effective echo train length. The NRGA parameters were specifically tuned for this MR-guided context.

**Findings:** The proposed technique was tested on phantom and human volunteer data with 240 views per breath-hold. Compared to conventional Cartesian acquisitions, the compressed sensing approach offered a significant acceleration factor of approximately 20x. Simulation studies indicated that an asymmetric view distribution (60 views in the craniocaudal direction and 48 in the phase-encode direction) yielded superior reconstruction quality. Consequently, the total views were allocated asymmetrically (55 and 45 views). Reconstructed 3D images and videos demonstrated high spatial fidelity, clear anatomic boundaries, and smooth temporal dynamics, confirming the method's efficacy. The technique was further validated on MR-guided radiotherapy phantom data.

**Conclusion:** An efficient 4D $T_2$-weighted imaging method has been developed. This approach enables the accurate measurement of respiratory motion in real-time with high spatial and temporal resolution, making it highly valuable for MR-guided interventions. The proposed protocol was well-received in both free-breathing volunteers and phantom setups, can be quickly programmed, and represents an improvement over prior methods. Ultimately, this technique is particularly well-suited for MR-guided interventions.

Rising inflation rates have driven individuals to shift funds from savings into stocks, commodities, and other investment avenues. Deep Learning models have repeatedly demonstrated their efficacy in forecasting time series data. Consequently, technical analysis utilizing various indicators remains a standard practice for traders and investors. Additionally, sentiment analysis of news and social media remains essential. However, these approaches remain largely reactive. Proactively generating alerts is even more valuable. Our research investigates these aspects within a deep learning framework that employs a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) for training a classifier to predict stock price movements. This setup involves a discriminator acting as the classifier and a generator creating fake data through interactions with the discriminator. The generator learns to produce data that indistinguishably mimics real price series by deceiving the discriminator. Ultimately, the model was evaluated on Google Stock, with results derived from both the discriminator and a probabilistic markov chain analysis of the generator's hidden states. These findings were validated against historical news and event-driven trends. Ultimately, the study's findings, news alignments, and alert mechanisms demonstrate clear practical utility. Consequently, the proposed approach offers a comprehensive analysis integrating historical data, sentiment, and event-driven insights using a generator-discriminator model. The discriminator provides predictions based on historical data and current events, while the generator offers projections based on hidden states and probabilistic markov chain analysis, also incorporating historical news and events. Crucially, the generator identifies connections between events and market movements by analyzing its own hidden states, a capability other models lack. This research employs a GAN to synthesize relevant data for prediction, a task for which GANs were not originally designed. Furthermore, the model was tested on recent market conditions, proving effective despite substantial geopolitical shocks. Abstract generation for stock price prediction represents a novel approach; the generator produces structured abstracts from news and events that capture their impact, which investors can monitor. This contrasts with conventional methods that merely feed raw data into a discriminator. By analyzing past events and their market effects via the generator's abstracts, traders can retrospectively analyze events and their consequences. The generator was tested against a baseline model, and the overall results were favorable.

There is a well-established history of designing property-preserving or structure-preserving discretization methods, such as energy stable finite element schemes for incompressible fluid flows, divergence-free spectral methods for nonlinear PDEs on the sphere, and mass-conserving schemes on graphs. This survey investigates the challenge of preserving properties on spectral methods with polynomial basis functions within the finite element framework, specifically examining high-order divergence-free spectral methods on computational grids for problems defined on geometrically complex domains. We provide an overview of existing literature, discuss key theoretical aspects, and include code demonstrations with quantitative results from a benchmark problem on periodic domains. While this work primarily utilizes a spectral polynomial approach for solution approximation, it also briefly addresses high-order discontinuous finite element methods. High-order divergence-free approximations on grids are essential for efficiently solving time-dependent PDEs on moderate to large-scale parallel computers, such as the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. On periodic domains, we have recently constructed such methods using a spectral polynomial approximation on a uniform grid, reducing the problem of finding a divergence-free velocity field to solving a system of linear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) for the pressure. This reduces the overall cost per time step by approximately an order of magnitude compared to traditional projection methods. This paper extends those methods to non-periodic domains, utilizing a spectral polynomial approximation via a multivariate orthogonal basis, such as tensor product Legendre polynomials, within a finite element context. We achieve this by decoupling the pressure solution from the standard weak formulation using a new mathematical operator inspired by operators in existing high-order divergence-free methods on periodic domains. This allows us to impose a discrete energy stability condition on the pressure solution. The method's accuracy, similar to a high-order finite element approach, can be readily increased by raising the polynomial order. This process involves aligning a preoperative CT-derived organ model with an intraoperative surface reconstructed from laparoscopic video. The task is complex due to factors such as sparse and noisy real-time data, numerous unknowns regarding tissue properties and boundary conditions, and the difficulty of establishing correspondences between pre- and intraoperative datasets. These challenges are exacerbated by the liver's lack of distinct surface features and the disparate noise characteristics of the imaging modalities used. To address this, we developed a convolutional neural network that simultaneously performs surface correspondence search and non-rigid registration. The network was trained on physically accurate biomechanical simulations of randomly generated, deforming organ-like structures, enabling immediate generalization to new patients without retraining. By incorporating varying levels of noise into the intraoperative surfaces during training, the model achieves robustness against noisy data. During inference, the network generates a displacement field that aligns the preoperative volume with the partial intraoperative surface. Experimental results demonstrate that the approach effectively translates to real-world data while maintaining high inference speed, and the source code is publicly available. The proposed method utilizes modern deep learning to create an end-to-end pipeline for non-rigid organ registration that ensures end-to-end physical plausibility and demonstrates strong generalization and robustness.

While these vectors are highly valuable for subsequent tasks like collision avoidance and action recognition, acquiring precise annotations for LiDAR and stereo camera data is both laborious and computationally expensive. To overcome this annotation barrier, we propose a solution on two fronts: a new 3D scene flow benchmark and a novel self-supervised training framework. This latent metric is optimized using a Multi-Scale Triplet loss that incorporates intermediary feature vectors. By applying our benchmark, we analyzed baseline and proposed model performances, discovering that our approach effectively maintains motion coherence and local geometry preservation—capabilities often lacking in other self-supervised methods. However, handling occlusions remains an unresolved challenge. To address this, we formulated an evaluation metric that assigns higher difficulty scores to scenarios with significant occlusions. We also note that enhancing the network's ability to handle highly occluded scenes represents a key area for future research. Regarding Hamiltonicity, we find that papillon graphs are Hamiltonian if and only a related "dove graph" is so; however, they always contain a non-Hamiltonian spanning subgraph composed solely of even cycles, confirming they are not Hamiltonian-connected. During runtime, Timeloops identifies which system calls a program should execute while blocking unauthorized attempts. It overcomes several limitations of current static analysis approaches, particularly in creating precise filters for interpreted languages like Python, PHP, and JavaScript. System call filtering offers a secure and efficient way to limit the behavior of applications and operating system components, serving as a foundational element in various security solutions, including the capability to systematically learn behavioral models for binaries and dynamic programs.

Wavefield reconstruction inversion (WRI) alleviates the requirement for strict adherence to the physical wave equation during iterations, whereas extended source waveform inversion (ESI) employs a non-physical source distributed across the computational domain that iteratively migrates toward the true physical source. Both WRI and ESI operate within a shared mathematical framework utilizing the Lagrangian-based adjoint-state method, with a specific emphasis on time-domain formulations using extended sources. Conceptually, WRI and ESI can be regarded as weighted variants of classical FWI. To efficiently solve the resulting normal equations in a matrix-free manner, the conjugate gradient method is applied, leveraging the symmetric positive definite Hessian; this approach supports both time and frequency domain wave equation solvers. However, the primary challenge remains the substantial storage requirements needed to retain time-domain wavefields throughout the iterative process. To address this, two strategies are proposed: extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data directly instead of wavefields. It is recommended that these approaches be further investigated to make these advanced imaging techniques more broadly applicable. Additionally, the corresponding Lagrangian formulations for the sparse frequency-domain methods and time-domain data strategies require development. While the described workflow represents one implementation, numerous modifications are feasible to enhance performance, such as integrating frequency-domain solvers, employing multigrid techniques, applying low-rank decompositions to the Hessian, and exploiting parallel computing capabilities. These enhancements can significantly improve the efficiency and scalability of the proposed workflow. Although the primary focus has been on waveform matching, this methodology is also suitable for scatterer parameter inversion. Furthermore, the high-resolution imaging capabilities of these advanced methods suggest they could potentially overcome the cycle skipping issues that often hinder standard inverse scattering techniques. Finally, the approach of storing wavefields at sparse spatial or temporal locations, rather than densely, represents a recently emerging time-saving technique in scattering imaging that warrants further exploration.

This study examines various designs aimed specifically at generating donut-shaped focal spots, a feature essential for trapping particles and atoms. By utilizing Rayleigh sum rules, we demonstrate that achieving a donut focal spot with any single-phase plate design—whether involving ring, spiral, or arc elements—is inherently limited, as these approaches can at best eliminate only half of the photons from the focal volume. Consequently, we introduce a novel two-element phase plate configuration capable of reducing the central 10% of photons in the focal volume, a significant improvement over current single-element options. This two-element design was validated through simulations of polystyrene particle trapping and experimental tests with atom traps. While modifications are necessary for different species, this two-element two-element phase plate design offers a practical and effective solution for particle trapping applications. Two-element phase plates are available open-source at https://github.com/MichaelSNowlin/DonutFocus. Advances in these devices can further enhance single-atom sensing, imaging, and trapping technologies. Advancement of such programmable two-element phase plates requires investment in research and development of electrostatic fabrication methods, including coated needle-in-ring, ring-with-branch, and spiral architectures. These developments enable optimized trapping within the smallest possible volume and are transferable to other physics, medical, and biological applications that require a focused donut profile. Abstract: Recent developments in programmable electrostatic phase plates have generated significant interest for specific applications. In this paper, we explore various designs intended to produce a donut-shaped focal spot, which is necessary for trapping particles and atoms. We apply Rayleigh sum rules to show that while a donut focal spot is the primary objective with any single-phase plate design—encompassing ring, spiral, or arc elements—this goal is intrinsically compromised, potentially removing only half of the photons from the focal volume. However, we present a new two-element phase plate design that achieves a donut focus and traps just 10% of the volume at the very center. This two-element design was tested for polystyrene particle trapping in simulation and for atom trapping experiments. Although adaptations are needed for different species, this two-element phase plate design is practical and effective for particle trapping. These two-element phase plates can also advance single-atom sensing, imaging, and trapping. Additionally, we present a comprehensive analysis of the spectrum resulting from the linearization around these solitary waves. This work extends the research of Sterbenz and Terashima and expands upon the findings of Sterbenz, Terashima, and Zhang. Our results demonstrate that standard index theorems are insufficient for determining the number of negative eigenvalues in the operator's spectrum. To address this, we develop a specialized "mountain pass" index theorem and apply it to count the unstable modes of the equation's solutions. Consequently, we are able to precisely characterize the stability or instability of every solitary wave based on the properties of its energy functional. We also provide a detailed account of our proof techniques, which leverage the explicit form of the linearized spectrum to derive sharp estimates on the geometry of the energy's level sets and sub-level sets. These findings extend the recent advancements by Sterbenz, Terashema, and Zhang concerning the instability of solitary waves in the one-dimensional $\mathbf{U}(1)$-invariant $\phi^4$ equation. Our primary tool is a novel application of variational methods, specifically a concentration-compactness alternative by Struwe, which splits the energy into compact and compactness-violating components. The non-compact nature of the latter is harnessed to show that, for a specific range of frequencies, the "mountain pass" index of the energy is at least as high as the index of a linearized eigenfunction associated with a positive eigenvalue.

Specifically, for a Galois extension K/Q where the Galois group G is isomorphic to A4, S4, or A5, we provide necessary and sufficient criteria for the ring of integers of K to be free over its corresponding order within the rational group algebra Q[G]. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these conditions are never met for S4 or A5. If f is a polynomial with coefficients in Z whose roots generate a Galois extension with group G, then the ring of integers is free over the integer order generated by Z and a generic element of G if and only if the Frobenius action on the 2-sylow quotient of the class group of this extension is semisimple. Our criteria are explicit and rely solely on the conjugacy class sizes of elements in G. We also offer similar, though less precise, criteria for groups isomorphic to A4. As applications, we resolve the freeness for numerous specific groups arising from polynomials with discriminant -24, 2304, or 81000. Additionally, these results have implications for the main conjecture in Iwasawa theory. The criteria developed here can be extended to any group isomorphic to a subgroup of S8.

This study examines the complementary nature of these signatures for the Belle II experiment, specifically focusing on axion-like particles ($a$) generated from meson decays. We introduce a novel approach to detect two-body decays characterized by $B^+ \to K^+ a$ followed by $a\to E\!\!\!/$, where $E\!\!\!/$ represents missing energy. Utilizing an integrated luminosity of $50\,$ab$^{-1}$, Belle II is capable of probing light invisible resonances with branching ratios $\mathcal{B}(B^+\to K^+ a) \gtrsim 10^{-7}$ and decay lengths $c\tau_a \gtrsim 1\,$m. For axion-like particles, we anticipate that the sensitivity of the $E\!\!\!/$ signature will improve by a factor of ten or more compared to current limits, largely due to the precise branching ratio measurement of $B^+\to K^+ a$ achieved through existing displaced-photon searches. We also analyze similar potentials for related ALP processes at Belle II, including $B_d^+ \to \mu^+ a$ and $B_s^+ \to \mu^+ a$. We detail the fundamental requirements for detecting such ALPs at Belle II and summarize the simple theoretical model parameters—defined by particle masses and four interaction coefficients—that allow ALPs to be produced at Belle II and probed through its detectors. The $B^+ \to K^+ E\!\!\!/$ signature offers a robust method to search for long-lived ALPs at Belle II, and this approach can be swiftly adapted to explore other neutral long-lived particle phenotypes, such as dark photons, within the same dataset.

We first introduce an ensemble method that surpasses prior contextualized approaches, which then serves as the foundation for a detailed analysis of predicted semantic shifts in English vocabulary over five decades. Our results indicate that these methods frequently assign high change scores to words that are not actually undergoing genuine diachronic semantic shifts, or where the validity of such shifts is dubious. We provide detailed discussions of these challenging instances with specific examples and propose corresponding linguistic classifications. Ultimately, we conclude that pre-trained contextualized language models tend to conflate changes in lexicographic senses with variations in contextual frequency, a bias inherent to their distributional nature that differs from issues seen in static embedding methods. Furthermore, these models often blend syntactic and semantic features of lexical items. Finally, we suggest several potential future solutions to address these problems. This research underscores the necessity of applying established evaluation frameworks, such as the SenseUr test battery, when assessing emerging NLP techniques for lexicographic and onomastic analyses. In this study, we utilize long-term, rapid lightsheet and two-photon imaging of zebrafish retinas *in vivo* during early development to identify the physical mechanisms driving nuclear behavior during IKNM. Our theory demonstrates that these fluids can maintain coherent motion, characterized by a non-zero mean velocity in the hydrodynamic limit, despite the disruptive effects of the disorder. Nevertheless, linearized hydrodynamics fails to capture the scaling behavior of these active systems in spatial dimensions ranging from 2 to 5. Despite this limitation, we derive the precise dimension-dependent scaling exponents for these ranges. These findings offer a rigorous methodology for calculating hydrodynamic parameters, such as mean square displacement and orientation correlation function, applicable to experiments and simulations involving incompressible polar active fluids with quenched disorder across various dimensions. This approach is especially significant for scenarios where dimensional reduction techniques are not feasible. We suggest that our methodology could be adapted to study other actively driven systems with extrinsic disorder. The proposed model and derived expressions are directly testable in current experiments involving photon-driven liquid crystals, microrobust swarms, and magnetotactic bacteria.

Amidst rising fraud in the current era, verification processes utilizing Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) for ID card extraction have been implemented to prevent account fraud. OCR technology converts images into text, enabling the extraction of data from Indonesian identity cards (KTP) to facilitate easier data entry for service operators. To enhance accuracy, NLP methods are employed to correct the extracted text. Testing on 50 Indonesian ID card images yielded an F-score of 0.78, with an extraction time of 4510 milliseconds per card. The implementation of this solution occurred at PT Adiprana for employee ID card data entry. Future enhancements could involve deep learning for improved extraction speed and accuracy, along with automatic data validation against a database to prevent duplicate accounts.

OCR is a process that transforms images containing text into machine-readable digital format. For Indonesian ID cards, extracting data into a structured format facilitates faster and more accurate processing. This approach mitigates the risk of account duplication, which is common due to human error in manual data entry. By automating this extraction, the potential for fraud is significantly reduced.

This project involves building a system to extract data from Indonesian ID cards using OCR and NLP technologies. The OCR implementation leverages Tesseract with Indonesian language support, while NLP tools assist in correcting extracted information. Data was tested on physical and digital Indonesian ID cards, with results demonstrating an F-score of 0.78, an accuracy of 0.87, a loss of 0.13, and a processing time of 4510 milliseconds. The system was deployed at PT Adiprana to streamline the ID data entry process. During deployment, the solution achieved an average processing time of 4400 milliseconds, an accuracy of 0.88, and an F-score of 0.77.

The deployment at PT Adiprana has lowered the average time required to input an ID card from approximately three minutes (using the previous manual method) to under one minute. This represents a 60% reduction in input time, significantly decreasing the likelihood of account duplication. The solution was ready for production one week after development began.

Keywords: OCR, NLP, ID Card Extraction, ID Card Data.

Expectation values of position were computed for different parameter combinations under a conventional ensemble. Expectation values sampled from this standard ensemble matched those obtained using a newly developed Monte Carlo method based on world lines. Furthermore, these results aligned with the classical solution derived via Laplace approximation. The proposed method is straightforward to implement and efficiently handles systems influenced by both constant and time-dependent forces. Because it does not rely on reweighting, it is well-suited for exploring landscapes of complex free energy functionals of path variables, such as in path integral variational approaches. Quantum Monte Carlo methods typically face difficulties when imaginary time depends on system parameters, such as when a potential includes a time-dependent driving field. This study introduces a world-line MC technique for calculating expectation values of operators in the Schrödinger equation with driven potentials. The method avoids the ergodicity problems that plague other approaches when potentials are driven. Since the technique does not assume a specific form for the driving potential, it is highly efficient for computations involving such potentials. Although the primary application concerns the expectation value of position, the approach is otherwise general and can be used to solve various problems, including the time-dependent Schrödinger equation with a driven harmonic oscillator or the evolution of wave functions under external driving fields within the time-dependent variational principle.

Expectation values of position operators were calculated for the Schrödinger equation with driven potentials using a new Monte Carlo method based on world lines. This approach does not require an adiabatic approximation, even when the driving potential takes a specific form. The technique is efficient because it does not increase computational cost with the amplitude of the drive, unlike other methods. The algorithm is broadly applicable, including to systems with harmonic friction and the Hubbard model. The proposed method is superior to previous techniques for calculating such expectation values because it avoids ergodicity breaking. Additionally, the approach does not depend on the specific form of the driving potential and can be readily extended to systems with multiple time-dependent parameters. Although the technique was developed to solve the time-dependent Schrödinger equation, it is not limited to this; it can also be applied to other contexts, such as evaluating coefficients in the expansion of the time-evolution operator into a Fourier series with respect to time.
