Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack (YORP) effect, a net torque generated by the reflection and thermal re-emission of solar radiation from their surfaces. This phenomenon causes a gradual alteration in rotation periods, which is most readily observable in light curves due to the quadratic accumulation of phase shifts over time. We gathered archived light curves and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids (10115) 1992 SK, (1620) Geographos, and (1685) Toro. Using light curve inversion, we fitted the data to convex shape models, modeling the YORP effect as a linear variation in rotation frequency ($\upsilon \equiv \mathrm{d}\omega / \mathrm{d}t$) and optimizing it alongside other spin and shape parameters. For asteroid (10115) 1992 SK, we detected a rotational acceleration of $\upsilon = (8.3 \pm 0.6) \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{rad}\,\mathrm{d}^{-2}$, which aligns well with theoretical predictions for its specific shape and spin model. Regarding (1685) Toro, we measured $\upsilon = (3.3 \pm 0.3) \times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{rad}\,\mathrm{d}^{-2}$; while generally consistent with literature values, it implies a slower spinning direction than previously recorded. We note that determining YORP acceleration from light curves becomes increasingly difficult as the acceleration approaches zero, which is why numerous known asteroids exhibit YORP accelerations greater than $10^{-8}\,\mathrm{rad}\,\mathrm{d}^{-2}$. Consequently, only future discoveries of slowly rotating (ulbyassov) asteroids will allow for more precise measurements of the YORP effect. In such cases, the object's spin will rapidly diverge from the prograde resonance regime, potentially triggering collisions with inner-solar-system asteroids or comets. Consequently, the YORP effect is believed to maintain a population of asteroids cleared from collisions near the 1:3 mean motion resonance with Jupiter.

A simplified variant, called next-generation reservoir computing (NGRC), further streamlines the process by eliminating many algorithmic hyperparameters to automatically identify high-performing traditional reservoir computers. This study examines a difficult scenario involving a dynamical system with multiple co-existing attractors and disparate time scales. By comparing NGRC and traditional reservoir computing using metrics that assess the geometry of both the true and predicted attractors, we analyzed a four-dimensional system. The study emphasizes that NGRC can learn complex systems featuring multiple co-existing attractors with significantly lower requirements for training data and hyperparameters than previous approaches. We encourage researchers to adopt this efficient method when learning any dynamical system, particularly in scenarios with low training data, high noise levels, or significant time scale separations. The mechanisms underlying the animacy continuum processed by the ventral temporal cortex (VTC) remain controversial. The visual categorization hypothesis posits that this continuum arises from the overlapping presence of animal and human features, whereas the social processing hypothesis attributes it to the prioritization of human-like stimuli. We experimentally tested the predictive power of both hypotheses. Participants rated the animacy of animal and human images, allowing us to model the continuum while factoring in the presence of human and animal features. Our results support both the visual categorization and social processing hypotheses. However, our data conflict with a recent extension of the social processing hypothesis, as the VTC responds to animals that lack any human features above a mid-point control condition. Consequently, we conclude that the visual categorization hypothesis provides a more parsimonious account of animacy. Additionally, we presented a novel paradigm capable of manipulating animal and human features independently, which can be used to further resolve disagreements regarding animal representation in VTC. This conclusion stems from a broader finding: Landau-Siegel zeros of Dirichlet $L$-functions cause the zeros of all other automorphic $L$-functions to repel from the line $\mathrm{Re}(s)=1$. Specifically, if a Dirichlet $L$-function possesses a zero at $1+\delta<1$, then the zeros of any other $L$-function are repelled from $\mathrm{Re}(s)=1$ with convergence rate $O(\delta^{c'})$ for some $c'>0$. Consequently, QE follows directly from the fact that landau-siegel zeros imply a strong level of Landau-siegel zeros. Our main consequence is a new criterion for quantum ergodicity on congruence groups $\Gamma_0(N)$. We note that while our approach does not yield the best possible exponent for QE (which stands at $1/4$ without assuming the absence of Landau-Siegel zeros), it provides an effective version of QE. Furthermore, our method yields a simpler proof of QE for large levels, previously established by Bernstein and Rudnick. The cornerstone of our approach is a new short sum formula for von Mangoldt functions, which also facilitates a shorter derivation of zero repulsion for other $L$-functions, as seen in related work by Blatter. This result extends and refines earlier findings by Soundararajan, Khare, Liou, and Wu.

This paper seeks to enhance the cross-task generalization capabilities of large-scale multi-task language models, such as T0 and FLAN, within an unsupervised framework. We introduce ReCross, a retrieval-augmentation approach that utilizes a few unlabeled examples as queries to fetch a targeted subset of upstream data, thereby updating the model to improve its generalization performance. ReCross represents a simple yet potent retrieval strategy that integrates efficient dense retrieval with effective pairwise reranking. Empirical results and analysis demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses both non-retrieval approaches and other baseline techniques. Specifically, compared to T0, our findings indicate that cross-task generalization relies on diverse data types and distribution patterns, actively "retrieving" data that complevers existing capabilities. Furthermore, by contrasting supervised and unsupervised settings, we observed that performance improvements stem from both increased task density and better parameterization. Finally, when applied to 20 NLP datasets across five different data domains using the T0 model, the average generalization performance was enhanced by more than 5 points beyond that achieved by other baselines.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into systems designed to execute code and interact with external environments. However, a significant challenge remains: ensuring that the data these models process is privacy-compliant. To address this, we propose a framework enabling LLMs to detect personally identifiable information (PII) within their inputs and either redact it or flag instances where privacy risks are high. Our approach combines a straightforward pipeline with advanced retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) techniques, offering a flexible solution that can be easily adapted to various datasets. We validate this framework across multiple scenarios, including public benchmarks and real-world datasets like GitHub repositories and Wikipedia pages. On the Wikipedia dataset, our results show that the RAG-based method outperforms baseline approaches by a substantial margin—exceeding 20 in F-score—and achieves a fivefold improvement over simple pipelines in detecting sensitive PII that users aim to keep private. Additionally, our work highlights the existence of "surface level PII," which is easily detectable and frequently appears in outputs generated by execution-friendly LLMs. This finding suggests that the perceived high frequency of PII on Wikipedia may be partly due to the ease with which models can extract such information. Finally, on the GitHub dataset, our method surpasses baseline performance by approximately 3 to 4 in F-score when detecting PII in Wikipedia

Consequently, there is a critical requirement for algorithms capable of efficiently identifying near-optimal hyperparameters that maximize privacy-utility tradeoffs within a defined search space. These values align with previous findings for the Sun-like stellar population analyzed in this study, as well as for high-latitude APOGEE-2 targets in DR16 and low-latitude populations in DR17. Ultimately, we conclude that the subtle spatial and chemical evolution of the Milky Way's disk is encoded within the scatter of abundance measurements.

During this period, online rumors heightened public anxiety regarding health and social stability, making the detection and containment of such misinformation an urgent priority. To address this, we investigated rumor propagation mechanisms and developed a method to quantify a rumor's influence based on the velocity of new adopters, utilizing search frequency as the primary metric. By analyzing this search frequency, which follows an exponential distribution, we calculated both peak and decay velocities. Furthermore, we introduced a new approach to measure the total scope of a rumor. Additionally, the derived parameters allow for the estimation of the proportion of individuals exposed to a rumor within a specific community, offering insights into why certain rumors gain rapid traction while others fade quickly. Finally, by leveraging the decay velocity, we proposed an algorithm to estimate the approximate number of people who encountered a rumor, as this value can be directly calculated from the model parameters. This research provides fundamental understanding of how rumors spread, serving as a foundation for future efforts to control their propagation. Consequently, during health crises, combating rumor-based misinformation becomes as critical as preventing viral infection. The proposed velocity measurement and typing method is particularly valuable for evaluating the impact of emerging rumors and can be readily applied to various communities, such as universities, where targeted anti-rumor campaigns can be deployed to effectively limit their spread.

the loss function plays a pivotal role, yet selecting the appropriate one remains challenging due to the vast array of available options. Despite this, related studies often fail to provide rigorous justifications for their specific choices, suggesting a dogmatic approach within the deep learning community that lacks empirical grounding. This work investigates supervised classification tasks to evaluate how loss function selection influences training outcomes. Although some functions yield suboptimal results, our empirical analysis demonstrates that underutilized losses, such as KL Divergence, can significantly surpass state-of-the-art alternatives. These findings underscore the necessity of treating the loss function as a tunable hyperparameter rather than adopting it as a fixed default. By framing the search for an optimal loss function as a combinatorial optimization problem, we developed a systematic method to efficiently evaluate all plausible combinations. Applied to 1,680 experiments across four datasets, our approach identifies the best configuration by prioritizing solutions with high empirical probability, a strategy that consistently yields favorable outcomes.

The analysis employs a Anderson-Hubbbard model featuring strong spin-orbit coupling on a honeycomb lattice, with the strength of the spin-orbit interaction beyond the bi-layer band structure being tunable. Using the dynamical mean-field theory of the local density functional, we investigate how the nematic symmetry, characterized by Crystalline Time-Reversal (CTR) symmetry, evolves under increasing external electric fields. Our results indicate that the spin-triplet nematic state collapses under relatively modest field strengths, returning to a conventional s-wave superconducting phase. Furthermore, we observe the emergence of a Mott insulator with a ferromagnetic state at high doping levels and strong external electric fields. Notably, the Hubbard $U$ value required to produce this ferromagnetic state is significantly lower than that needed for a spin-triplet nematic state, a finding that contradicts the general understanding of ferromagnetism in itinerant systems, which typically demands a much stronger Hubbard $U$. This paradox arises because the CTR-symmetric spin-triplet nematic state favors an orbital state with $d$-wave symmetry, which enhances spin polarization and thereby promotes ferromagnetism. These discoveries provide a detailed account of the phase diagram, detailing the transitions between the spin-triplet nematic, s-wave, and ferromagnetic states, alongside the associated changes in order parameter symmetries and electronic properties. Consequently, Bi$_2$Se$_3$ offers a distinctive mechanism for generating a ferromagnetic state, which could be harnessed to create a spin-transistor utilizing a moderate Hubbard $U$. The key to this unusual behavior lies in the specific symmetry of the spin-triplet nematic state, a phenomenon potentially accessible through chemical doping or lattice distortions in other topological insulators. Despite these advantages, it exhibits a signal-to-noise ratio deficit compared to optimal coherent detection. This paper enhances the error rate performance of standard differential detection by employing a delay interval exceeding one symbol period. This was originally established by computing noise kernels, which represent the correlators of the stress-energy tensor for quantum fields. This paper revisits the topic using a quantum thermodynamic framework, specifically calculating two key quantities: heat capacity and quantum compressibility for model geometries containing quantum fields at both high and low temperatures. Heat capacity at constant volume serves as a measure of energy density fluctuations relative to the mean; when this ratio reaches or exceeds one, the applicability of the canonical distribution becomes doubtful. Similarly, compressibility at constant pressure acts as a test for the validity of the grand canonical ensemble. We derive the free energy density to obtain expressions for these thermodynamic quantities for thermal and quantum fields across various spacetimes, including 2D Casimir space, the 2D Einstein cylinder, and the 4D ($S^1 \times S^3$) Einstein universe. To differentiate between causes and effects, agents and themes, voluntary versus involuntary events, and actions versus mental states, we define approximately 20 distinct if-then relation types. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism (BiAM) that utilizes a multi-modal learning approach to jointly train the bottom layers of an ASR encoder and a text encoder. BiAM facilitates the exchange of feature sampling rates, ensuring that transformed features from one modality are accurately evaluated within the other's space using diversified objective functions. To validate the method's effectiveness, we conducted experiments on the Librispeech and CNN/testset datasets. To address the issue of lacking parallel data, we integrated a knowledge distillation strategy during pre-training, allowing the model to learn from unlabeled text data by leveraging a teacher network that provides high-quality multi-modal representations. Our experiments demonstrate that BiAM significantly outperforms baseline approaches, yielding an additional 1.3% CER reduction compared to conventional unimodal learning methods. The final model, enhanced by distillation using a teacher network (approximately 300M parameters), achieves accurate transcription on the CNN/testset with a low CER of 18.5% when trained solely on Librispeech data. Although these findings align qualitatively with predictions regarding quantum interference among coherent phase slip components, the observed tuning period exceeds simple capacitance-based estimates by several orders of magnitude. We also evaluate the viability of an explanation attributing this behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowire. Ultimately, we offer updated predictions for theoretical models, incorporating all observed characteristics, microscopic proximity effect calculations, and insights from a single-nanowire experiment. Our analysis indicates that the data can be accounted for by granular Josephson junctions activating or bypassing a phase slip box; however, the derived parameters present significant challenges for this scenario to remain consistent with our proximity effect measurements. We conclude that, although generic granular models struggle to explain the observations, coherent quantum phase slips remain inherently robust and can operate across a broad spectrum of environmental conditions.

This study investigates airborne infection risks on an urban bus by employing unsteady Reynolds-Averaged Navier--Stokes equations alongside a passive-scalar model for virus-laden aerosol concentrations. Furthermore, the study finds that the bus is not well-mixed, as infections are more likely to occur between passengers who are close together. While mechanical ventilation tends to push viruses toward the windows and reduce overall concentrations, it may inadvertently increase the infection risk to specific passengers. Additionally, because thermal plumes from engines and passengers can concentrate viruses in certain areas, keeping windows closed is recommended to mitigate these effects. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, including graphene and ferromagnetic layers. Manipulating spin-orbit coupling offers a potential route to uncover novel and exotic phases within superconducting and semimetallic systems. In this study, we investigate the magnetoelectrical transport properties—specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect—in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers to identify signatures of the spin-orbit proximity effect and determine its origin. Our findings suggest an increase in the intrinsic contribution to the anomalous Hall effect from the Bismuth layers due to the Cobalt deposits, indicating that the effect arises from scattering between the two components rather than a change in the scattering mechanism. Furthermore, we propose a model grounded in the Hall effect scattering scenarios to semiquantitatively describe these magnetoelectrical transport signatures. Additionally, we highlight that spin-hall magnetoresistance serves as a viable method for detecting the spin-orbit proximity effect in Cobalt thin layers integrated within Bismuth films. Ultimately, by combining our results with first-principles calculations, we conclude that this effect in Cobalt thin layers planted on Bismuth substrates is driven by surface spin-orbit scattering. This conclusion aligns with the widely accepted mechanism for the spin-orbit proximity effect in graphene on heavy metals, which is also surface-driven. However, we emphasize a key distinction: in graphene, the effect results from renormalization, whereas in Cobalt, it stems from surface scattering. These insights provide a comprehensive understanding of the spin-orbit proximity effect in both itinerant electrons and localized magnetic moments. The methodology and conclusions presented here are original contributions and may prove instrumental in elucidating the effect in other magnetic materials.

We propose an operational definition of centering and employ a search-based methodology to systematically evaluate whether neural coreference resolvers comply with CT rules through various discourse metrics. To facilitate future research, we open the field by releasing the first coreference task trained and evaluated with centering as both a training objective and an evaluation metric. WiFi fingerprinting, which involves gathering Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) measurements at known locations, is a prevalent technique in various positioning algorithms found in existing literature. However, accurately calculating the spatial distance between fingerprints is highly dependent on the choice of signal distance function, a parameter that often lacks clear guidance in research papers. This study proposes two key contributions. First, it establishes that the absolute maximum error in location estimation, expressed as the discrepancy between the estimated and actual distances between fingerprints, directly dictates the scaling factor (meters per dB) of the linearized distance model used to compute final coordinates; this maximum error is observed to lie between 3 and 5 meters. Second, the authors demonstrate that proving the positivity of semidefinite matrices enables the formulation of a nonlinear optimization problem to determine the Euclidean geometry of a space based of the relative distances between fingerprints, thereby eliminating the need for arbitrary signal distance function parameters. Simulation results, along with evaluations on two real-world datasets, confirm the accuracy of these findings. Additionally, the study offers practical recommendations for deploying WiFi fingerprinting systems, including how to select locations for measurement collection and which signal distance metrics to utilize.

In this study, we examine the one-loop six-gluon amplitude within $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills (SYM) theory under a central next-to-multi-Regge kinematic (NMRK) limit. We demonstrate that the dispersive part of this amplitude factorizes using the two-gluon CEV, allowing us to derive the one-loop two-gluon CEV for all helicity configurations in this theory. While computed in the NMRK limit, this configuration can be extended to the standard next-to-Regge kinematic setup by employing effective theory techniques for higher-point amplitudes. Finally, we provide the explicit formula for the two-gluon CEV when all external gluons share the same negative helicity. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first calculation of a two-gluon CEV in the general helicity configuration for any tree-level plus ladder diagram topology. This result significantly advances the pathway to computing next-to-leading logarithmic (NLL) real emission contributions within effective field theories for high-energy scattering. However, directly applying this finding to Fadin's effective field theory (feBFKL) encounters an obstacle: the two-gluon CEV involves elliptic functions of the color ordering, whereas feBFSL is defined only for rational functions. Overcoming this hurdle will enable the application of feBFKL to predict high-energy scattering properties of beyond standard model physics beyond the Large Hadron Collider, as suggested by recent findings. To achieve this, one must extend feBFKL to a generalized version capable of incorporating the two-gluon CEV. Additionally, adapting the method presented in this paper to other multi-leg amplitudes could facilitate this extension. Ultimately, completing these tasks will allow for the calculation of NNLL radiation corrections in effective theories for high-energy scattering, which can serve as probes for new physics at the high energies anticipated at the High-Luminosity LHC. To our awareness, this paper introduces several original concepts and methods that are potentially applicable to other scattering scenarios involving high-energy particles.

Nevertheless, the parabolic approximation cannot accurately describe polymers attached to convex, curved substrates, such as spherical nanoparticles or interfaces within strongly segregated block copolymers. Prior research demonstrated that strongly stretched brushes on curved surfaces necessitate a boundary layer free of chain ends, prompting revisions to the theoretical framework. Although this "end exclusion zone" has been integrated into models for brushes on cylinders and spheres, the behavior on surfaces with arbitrary curvature remains unexplored. This work introduces a strong-stretching theory formulation for molten brushes on surfaces of arbitrary curvature and identifies four distinct regimes where end exclusion zones occur, including cases with positive mean but negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching equations, we characterize the scaling of end exclusion zone size, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and stretching free energy relative to mean and Gaussian curvatures. These findings provide a comprehensive understanding of how brush geometry dictates end exclusion zones and exact strong-stretching free energies, offering a framework applicable to modeling the full range of brush geometries found in block copolymer melt assembly. Furthermore, we contrast our strong-stretching formulation with recent weak-stretching molecular field theory simulations on spheres, validating the new approach. Finally, we propose that our formulation can resolve discrepancies between prior weak-stretching simulations and mean-field simulations on curved surfaces. Mean curvature always induces end exclusion zones, while extremal Gaussian curvature regimes define the boundaries for the two most unusual zones that lack a strong-stretching limit. On nanoparticle assemblies and other periodic structures with curved interfaces, these end exclusion zones can significantly influence the chemical potential balance required to stabilize multiple micellar phases. Our findings are directly relevant to experiments involving the assembly of polymers on nanoparticle superlattices, the formation of mesoscopic domains in block copolymer melts, and the creation of curved interfaces on high-curvature nanoscale objects. Strong-stretching simulations on various curved surfaces offer a robust, efficient method to explore the full spectrum of brush geometries inherent to block copolymer melts, aiding in the design of micellar mesostructures. Additionally, this formulation enables the investigation of pinning energies associated with micellar interface defects on high-curvature nanoscale protrusions or impurities to accurately determine defect mobility. Beyond applications to block copolymer melts, this formulation may prove useful for analyzing other mesoscopic phenomena involving pinning by high-curvature interfaces

We attempted to synthesize a one-year ASM from a short-exposure, one-week observation dataset using three ML-based image processing techniques: dictionary learning, U-net, and a new method termed ML-ASMap (ML-based mapping of all-sky). The proposed ML-ASMap method functions by independently fitting a model to the photon count rate distribution across the entire map, representing count rates in every sky direction via mathematical expressions (e.g., a polynomial model). Subsequently, ML techniques generate images by combining models from all sky directions. Validation against a one-year ASM confirmed that this approach achieves comparable results to existing methods for ASMs. Furthermore, this method offers a significant advantage for studies investigating time-variable sources: it requires no assumption that sources remain constant over time and demands less data for implementation. Specifically, a one-week exposure suffices to produce high-quality maps for time-resolved studies, a period easily monitored for transients using all-sky monitors like IACTs. When detecting transient events, only the models from regions surrounding the event need to be refitted, substantially reducing the computational load. We will apply this method to identify new variable sources within the Galactic center. Given its potential utility in time-resolved analyses, this approach is especially beneficial when examining periods for variable phenomena in studies of specific astronomical targets.

Each agent selects an action to maximize her own value, conditioned on the choices made by preceding agents. Our objective is to identify action sequences that achieve a total social welfare close to the optimal solution. We assume the ability to query the value $v_i(S)$ obtained by agent $i$ when acting after the set of agents $S$. We derive tight bounds on the social welfare achievable with a polynomial number of queries. While these general bounds indicate only a marginally sublinear approximation of optimal welfare, significantly better approximations emerge when valuations originate from specific combinatorial structures. For instance, when valuations correspond to bipartite matchings, directed graph arborescences, or Boolean satisfiability, simple query-efficient algorithms achieve a $2$-approximation. We also address truthfulness concerns, demonstrating how certain algorithms can be made truthful via VCG-like payments. Furthermore, we define and analyze the "price of serial dictatorship," a metric offering an optimistic assessment of the solution quality produced by action sequences in combinatorial optimization. Finally, we examine the performance of our proposed algorithms across various standard combinatorial settings, such as travel salesperson tours and maximum weight independent sets. Our main contribution lies in introducing this abstract framework, which enables the design of high-quality algorithms for specific instances, and in highlighting the substantial disparity between the potential of serial dictatorship in a query-free, boolean world versus its performance when realistic valuation queries are required. These techniques were implemented using data from the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE), which features a 100 milliJanskys sensitivity at 12 and 2.4 micrometers with sufficient photometric accuracy for PSM analysis. At near-CRWIS places (close to the saturation limit for WISE), we established that the maximum resolvable binary separation is determined not by image FWHM or detector pixel size, but by the width of the wings in the PSF. Consequently, we can detect binary asteroids with separations up to ~1.5 arcseconds at 12 um and up to ~2.5 arcseconds at 2.4 um. At fainter magnitudes, the primary asteroid's PSF saturates while the secondary remains unsaturated, causing the secondary to appear as a dip adjacent to the primary's image center. We developed two programs to automatically find these wide-separation binaries: the First method compares the spectral energy distribution (SED) of known single asteroids against a grid of two-body models, leveraging the accurate secondary measurements to identify mismatches in the primary's flux. The second approach utilizes a machine learning classifier (Random Forest) trained on synthetic images to scan for two-body systems. At 12 um, we can recover secondaries as faint as 2.5 magnitudes weaker than the primary, and at 2.4 um, we can detect secondaries up to 3.0 magnitudes fainter. We tested these methods on a sample of 10,000 known single asteroids at 12 um and 20,000 at 2.4 um, finding that approximately 0.2% of asteroids at 12 um and 0.6% at 2.4 um exhibit clear binary signatures. At 2.4 um, about 10% of the identified binaries consist of a non-resolving primary and a secondary with a diffraction-spread flux. We compiled a list of 10,000 new wide-separation binary asteroids at 12 um and 20,000 at 2.4 um, many of which are likely new discoveries. These objects can be further examined with high-sensitivity instruments on large telescopes to determine if they are double asteroids or binary asteroid systems with wider separations. At 2.4 um, we also have the capability to detect smaller secondary bodies

Recent research categorizes the topology and geometry of knotted proteins by examining the distribution of their planar projections through topological entities known as knotoids. We adopt a similar analytical framework by developing a topologically grounded statistical metric to compare knotoid distributions among proteins sharing the same topology. Our method identifies geometric variations between trefoil proteins by quantifying their entanglement and successfully recovers clusters based on sequence similarity. By directly investigating the geometry and topology of native states, we can explore distinct folding pathways in proteins that form open-ended trefoil knots. Notably, our pipeline indicates that the folding process of shallowly knotted Carbonic Anhydrases involves the formation of a double-looped structure, a finding that contrasts with previous observations regarding deeply knotted trefoil proteins. We corroborate these results using Molecular Dynamics simulations. Furthermore, we establish that the proportion of planar projections yielding the minimum energy state for the primary knot differs between these two protein types and directly influences their folding timescales. Modifying a local, unknotted region within the protein backbone can significantly alter both the proportion of planar projections and the folding dynamics of the knotted domain. Our simulated proteins, composed of amino acid chains with designed sequences and structures, demonstrate that a substantial fraction of planar projections involving the deeply knotted minimum energy state (approximately 25%) is essential for achieving fast folding dynamics (around 200 nanoseconds). However, a higher fraction (approximately 50%) is required for the shallowly knotted case to achieve even faster folding (around 10 nanoseconds). Our discovery of this distinct folding mechanism in shallowly knotted proteins offers a novel perspective on the relationship between a protein's folded state and its folding dynamics, a hypothesis that can be tested using currently available protein design techniques.

The investigation focuses on mathematical foundations spanning Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The basis of the NG boson counting law in the anomalous context is explored through both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. A quasi-Heisenberg algebra is identified as a generic feature across various symmetry-breaking schemes of the anomalous NG theorem; this algebra suggests a violation or modification of the Heisenberg uncertainty relation within the NG sector, a phenomenon that is potentially verifiable experimentally. The formalism of the effective potential is introduced to elucidate the mechanism of the anomalous NG theorem using the derived Lie algebra results. Following an examination of a bosonic kaon condensation model incorporating a finite chemical potential as an explicit Lorentz-symmetry-breaking parameter, a general model Lagrangian approach to the anomalous NG theorem is proposed. This analysis not only determines the conditions for the counting law of true NG bosons but also reveals the mechanism for generating the mass of massive NG bosons. Furthermore, the emergence of a massive mode in the NG sector is interpreted through the quantum uncertainty relation of the Heisenberg algebra, which arises from Lie algebra symmetry breaking and is realized within the effective potential of the kaon condensation model. Additional examples from literature are discussed using the formalism established in this work, with their results analyzed via the uncertainty relation of the emergent Heisenberg algebra. Finally, implications of this mechanism for generating the masses of massive NG bosons in physical scenarios, such as superfluids and astrophysical neutron stars, are investigated. The methodology and findings of this paper may serve as a theoretical framework for studying other matter-construction models in high-energy physics, condensed matter physics, and related fields. Ultimately, this technique enables the epitaxial growth of various functional materials with substantial lattice mismatches (>10%) and facilitates the creation of pinhole-free, epitaxially aligned heterostructures on costly substrates. Ultimately, this bulk heteroepitaxy technique expands the range of epitaxial materials and enables the integration of multiple functional heterostructures, utilizing expensive substrates efficiently and recycling them after membrane extraction.

Quantile Cross Validation (QCV) is noted as a promising direction for future research. On a dataset containing classes with varying sample counts, QCV offers a robust train/test split strategy that outperforms traditional methods, particularly in imbalanced learning scenarios where multiple classes exist. Recently, there has been growing interest in applying Natural Language Processing (NLP) technologies to analyze conversations and interactions. The proposed work introduces a novel approach to automatically tag dialogues with structured information relevant to Information Extraction tasks. This methodology was experimentally applied to extract structured data from free-text explanations provided by university admissions officers regarding their decisions. Our experiments on real data demonstrate that modern Neural Network approaches can effectively learn to tag explanations with structured data, even when trained on relatively small datasets. These results highlight the potential for applying NLP methods and techniques to analyze interactions across various domains and contexts.

University recruiting systems are increasingly utilizing the web to engage applicants. Our study examines a system designed to streamline the selection and communication phases of the recruitment process for highly skilled professionals. This system plans the entire workflow—from scheduling reviews and interviews to coordinating their conduct—with the ultimate goal of producing a standardized output suitable for a decision maker. Although the system addresses distinct problems regarding panel creation and scheduling, it accounts for interactions and dependencies between these components to ensure a fully automated process. Our findings indicate that utilizing a heuristic algorithm, specifically a generalized version of the Largest First Approach, yields superior results when planning the university recruiting process. This represents a significant advancement over previous work, which often treated these problems independently. Furthermore, the system is constructed with a modular architecture that facilitates the integration of additional features, thereby providing a robust foundation for future enhancements.

venshtein introduced the sequence reconstruction problem, which examines a scenario where an identical sequence is sent multiple times through independent, identically distributed, symmetric binary erasure channels. The receiver's task involves recovering the original sequence from these transmissions, leveraging the fact that sent symbols can be inferred from repeated symbol occurrences. This paper analyzes the optimal reconstruction rate, denoted as $R^{*}($\theta)$, for this process, defined as the minimum number of transmissions required so that the probability of error does not exceed $\theta \in [0,1]$. Asymptotically, for large sequences, the dominant factor influencing error probability is determined by the event where a received sequence contains no occurrence of a zero symbol pattern that would cause ambiguity. This finding provides an explicit upper bound on $R^{*}($\theta)$ and, combined with a previously established lower bound, shows that the reconstruction rate grows logarithmically with sequence length. Numerical results indicate that the base of this logarithm ranges between 1.7 and 2. The study also explores modifications to the standard model, including a time-limited variant and a version with correlated sources, demonstrating that both exhibit a linear growth of the optimal reconstruction rate. Furthermore, the research investigates the optimal rate for a "bit reconstruction" objective, showing it follows a quadratic dependence on the error threshold $\theta$. Finally, the paper considers a generalization of the sequence reconstruction problem to a channel with memory and elucidates its connection to the codeword reconstruction issue in such channels. The findings hold significance for understanding data recovery from redundant transmissions, which is relevant to various engineering applications.

Expanding our capacity to detect and characterize gravitational waves is vital for advancing our understanding of general relativity and the sources emitting them. A primary method for detecting high-amplitude signals is through timing arrays. This approach involves measuring the arrival times of pulsar pulses with microsecond precision, as gravitational waves traveling from the sky to Earth will induce measurable delays. Because these signals are generally non-Gaussian and have not been observed before, identifying them requires accurate modeling of all potential foreground influences. This includes precisely mapping the motion of Solar System bodies that generate well-known effects, as well as other signals originating from within our own or other galaxies. We begin by outlining the fundamental characteristics of the classic Kermack-McKendrick models before exploring their generalizations and applications to contact networks, viral co-circulation, epidemic curve trajectories, probability distributions, passage times, passage curve dynamics, infection severity, incubation, recovery, and mortality. Collectively, these models define the system's state through state space, state variable vector, and state dimension. We also analyze parameter space and its segments, focusing on the basic reproduction number as a primary driver of disease spread and its impact on the number of infected individuals. Furthermore, we discuss estimates of the basic reproduction number derived from empirical data collected throughout the pandemic, along with strategies to reduce it below one. This process involves reviewing control measures, their measures of effectiveness, and their effects on infected population dynamics, as well as control theory approaches to optimal control. We consider control variables subject to constraints, their time-dependent behavior, and the objective function used to minimize infection counts and control costs. The study further investigates the basic properties of an optimal control problem, including its objective, constraints, state space, and cost functional, and applies Pontryagin's Maximum Principle to derive the necessary conditions of optimality known as the adjoint system. We conclude with a numerical simulation analyzing the pandemic in Ghana from pre-pandemic conditions through March 2021, covering infection, hospitalization, intensive care, and mortality data, as well as the effectiveness of various control measures. The final section offers suggestions for future research. Throughout, our objective has been to demonstrate the utility of different Kermack-McKendrick models and their roles in formulating policies and strategies to combat the pandemic. By utilizing empirical data, these models help decision-makers evaluate control measures and their impacts, assess risks associated with the virus, and determine strategies to lower the basic reproduction number below one, thereby ending the epidemic. Ultimately, we emphasize that while these models are based on deterministic ordinary differential equations and can be extended to stochastic models, their primary goal remains controlling the pandemic. However, we note that models exist for every phenomenon, and selecting the most appropriate model for pandemic management is an ongoing area of research that requires consideration of additional models and methods, such as those utilizing fractional derivatives to better fit empirical data. Ultimately, our focus remains on controlling the pandemic rather than engaging in model competitions.

Specifically, we analyze how, under appropriate dark-state conditions, the interaction between spin-exchange collisions and photoassociation facilitates the stable formation of atom-molecule pairs from three initial spin-zero atoms. This mechanism, involving two distinct two-body interactions, can be conceptually understood as an effective three-body recombination. We explore the respective influences of photoassociation and initial magnetization in the "resonant" scenario where the dark-state condition is perfectly met. Additionally, we investigate the "non-resonant" regime, where this condition is either approximately fulfilled (the adiabatic case) or not met at all. In the adiabatic scenario, we develop an effective non-rigid pendulum model that enables a clear discussion of the emergence of antiferromagnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum," alongside phenomena such as large-amplitude pair oscillations and atom-molecule entanglement. Finally, we consider the far non-resonant case, offering both a qualitative account and a perturbative treatment that reveals mirror-pendulum-like behaviors and exotic fractionated spins resembling magnetic spins in Kondo impurity or Kramers crystal systems. These discoveries suggest potential applications in manipulating complex interactions among bosonic atom-molecule pairs via photoassociation, thereby enabling the engineering of effective Hamiltonians for spin-1 Bose-Einstein condensates that include atom-molecule pairing terms. Consequently, the effective physics of a atom-molecule pendulum or a Kondo-like impurity can be realized, providing a novel pathway to investigate quantum entanglement of massive particles and the magnetism of heavy particles.

This design also overcomes the limitations of earlier systems, which struggled with update operations and were largely restricted to appending new data. By leveraging a hierarchical index stored in an abundant four-base-overhead encoding, our system achieves a practical addressable space exceeding 10 petabytes (PeBs) while maintaining a high fundamental addressable capacity of 1 terabase (TbEs). We demonstrate a flexible data unit capacity ranging from 100 gigabytes (GBs) to 100 terabytes (TBs), with an optimal 10-terabyte (TB) unit achieving high addressable capacities of 1.1 PeBs and 1.3 PeBs for random and sequential access, respectively. Beyond its utility for data updates, this architecture is particularly well-suited for time-series data and multimedia processing. We have open-sourced the software implementation of this architecture (project page: https://github.com/NovotnTeam/DNAstore) to demonstrate a 1,000-fold increase in addressable space for large data units, surpassing current state-of-the-art capabilities. Furthermore, our system utilizes a high-capacity four-base encoding, substantially reducing the actual stored volume for sequential access and offering a cost-effective solution for sequential data access. Overall, this framework provides a comprehensive and adaptable solution for future high-capacity DNA storage applications.

While the Saint-Venant equations offer a widely used framework for velocity prediction, they require complex numerical solutions that depend on intricate flow geometry and extensive initial/boundary data. These factors often hinder real-world predictions, particularly in emergency scenarios. This study introduces a new 1D linearized shallow water model specifically designed for flat river sections with constant geometry and steady flow. The approach yields an explicit velocity solution that, given the regular nature of river banks, can be rapidly computed even during flood events. Furthermore, this linearized model can be integrated into more general systems of equations. Numerical simulations demonstrate that this new method produces velocity predictions that align closely with both numerical solutions of the Saint-Venant equations and actual measurements derived from river depth and slope. The approach is especially effective for medium-to-long term flow velocity predictions, as it requires only depth and slope at the domain inlet and average geometric properties (cross-sectional area and wetted perimeter), which can be pre-calculated and easily measured. Consequently, this method is ideal for field deployments, such as utilizing imaging laser sensors on river banks to forecast flow velocities based on easily measurable parameters. The code is written in Python, and the linearized model can be expanded to handle non-prismatic flows by computing the explicit velocity solution over short river segments with nearly constant geometry, thereby creating a rapid Saint-Venant solver for velocity that complements the solver developed in our previous work. Python sources for both the linearized and non-linearized solvers are available at https://github.com/ElieTouran/SV_source_wave_celerity. We encourage researchers and practitioners to employ this efficient method for velocity estimation, either independently or alongside our earlier linearized model that accounts for variable bed slope and river width.

significant and emerging subfield within machine learning, focused on embedding causal knowledge into the highly adaptable spaces of deep learning architectures. Successfully integrating these causal structures promises more robust, generalizable, and informed predictions and inference. However, the field remains nascent, particularly regarding how to evaluate disparate methods that differ vastly in their output formats, encoding mechanisms, and representation strategies. This living paper extends Pearl's ladder of causation by refining its levels and introducing a new dimension to categorize parametric assumptions for both inputs and representations, thereby creating a comprehensive map of causal deep learning. This framework encompasses various machine learning domains, including supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling. Designed as a research tool, the map assists scholars in locating benchmarks, comparing methodologies, and, crucially, identifying gaps in current research. While the volume of published work on CDL grows daily, this map remains static. We have open-sourced the map to facilitate its use by the community, whether for structuring related work sections or more effectively highlighting specific contributions.

known as oriented colored broken submersions. This category represents the most fundamental class of maps adhering to a version of the $h$-principle; in two dimensions, it closely approximates oriented submersions, as every such map of dimension 2 targeting a closed, simply connected manifold is bordant to a submersion. We demonstrate that the Madsen-Weiss theorem (the standard Mumford Conjecture) operates within a broader framework of the $h$-principle. Specifically, a version of the $h$-principle for oriented colored broken submersions, when combined with the Harer stability theorem and the Miller-Morita theorem, yields the Madsen-Weiss theorem. This approach was inspired by the solution to the Massey version of the $h$-principle for submersions by V. Tamara. Moreover, an analogous argument can be applied to establish the Kontsevich-Block Gromov $h$-principle regarding submersions. Consequently, an effective procedure exists to determine whether a given map from the configuration space of points on a surface to a differential graded algebra (representing the cohomology of a manifold) is realizable by a submersion. This provides a significant step toward solving the long-standing problem of whether a specific DGA is isomorphic to the quantum cohomology of a manifold. Additionally, the paper offers a concise review of the various formulations of the $h$-principle for submersions found in existing literature.

Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) preconditioners applied to cardiac mechanics on both structured and unstructured finite element meshes. Myocardial mechanical behavior is modeled using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, which are discretized via finite elements to generate large-scale nonlinear algebraic systems. These systems are solved using a Newton-Krylov method, with BDDC/AMG preconditioners accelerating the resolution of the Jacobian linear systems. To ensure a fair comparison, we comprehensively investigate key BDDC parameters, optimizing their settings for a specific large-scale problem. The results demonstrate that a carefully configured BDDC preconditioner matches the performance of a sophisticated AMG preconditioner, requiring approximately 2 hours of wall-clock time over four time steps for a human heart simulation on 16,000 processors using unstructured meshes. This scenario involves a nonlinear material law, thick tissues, and the elimination of pressure degrees of freedom. Additionally, the study analyzes the performance of both BDDC and AMG across various scenarios, offering insights into their efficiency at different time discretization steps, polynomial degrees, and mesh sizes. Specifically, when the finite element approximation is coarse, a BDDC preconditioner with a few thousand blocks exhibits significant superconvergence, reducing the iteration count by nearly half compared to AMG. These findings are derived from an extensive set of numerical experiments. The code is based on OpenSource Chaste, with the BDDC implementation developed specifically for this project. This project is also designed to aid others in implementing and testing BDDC for their own applications. The code is further enhanced to compare BDDC performance against AMG in terms of solution time, memory usage, and convergence. The implementation achieves high performance by utilizing scalable library components: Jacobian assembly and application utilize SCOTCH for graph partitioning, MPI for all inter-process communication, and PETSc for BDDC, AMG, and time stepping. BDDC performance is assessed by examining the density of the Schur system and the density of BDDC Jacobian blocks. The analysis of BDDC performance relies on metrics such as the density of the original and BDDC-factored finite element meshes, as well as the density of BDDC primary variables. Performance is measured relative to three factors: the density of primary variables, the density of the finite element mesh, and the complexity of the material law. Finally, the study compares these findings against performance predictions made by Jacobian analysis, BDDC theory

This study examines the dispersion of a population of fractional Brownian walkers, which exhibit long-time correlations and possess time-dependent, heterogeneous diffusivity. The goal is to derive the scenarios arising from these individual-level characteristics by analyzing the temporal evolution of the population's spatial distribution. We investigate the feasibility of obtaining a Markovian description of this process to understand how "apparent" long-range correlations emerge from localized short-range memory. By contrasting these findings with previous research on process-level correlations, we clearly distinguish between process and process Derivative Long Memory (pDLM) and agent Long Memory (LM) and agent Derivative Long Memory (DLM). This comparison highlights the risks of misinterpreting memory types when only pDLM is considered. While we show that fractional Brownian dynamics can generate DLM, we also identify scenarios where such dynamics produce a combination of LM and 1/f noise that is not Markovian. To better characterize these non-Markovian dynamics, we introduce an apparent fractal dimension (AFD) as a tool for quantifying memory on a process level. To elucidate the mechanisms behind these apparent long-range correlations, we use an agent-based model with short-memory dynamics that mimics the non-Markovian dynamics of fractional Brownian walkers. This model features a time-dependent diffusivity governed by the square of the agent's displacement from the mean square displacement of a standard Brownian walker, allowing us to isolate the mechanism of apparent long-range correlations and confirm that the AFD always exceeds 1. This confirms that any process exhibiting LM, regardless of its underlying mechanism, will display 1/f noise. However, we note that 1/f processes are inherently Markovian only when viewed on long timescales, as they can be described by an infinite hierarchy of nested Markovian processes. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for analyzing the dynamics of active matter and other systems involving agents.

addresses both linear and Kerr nonlinear couplings among modes in dielectric optical resonators. Because this approach is independent of specific geometries or mode bases, it serves as a versatile foundation for analyzing phenomena arising from any mix of linear coupling, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity. These include losses due to bending and surface roughness, geometric backscattering, self- and cross-phase modulation, four-wave mixing, third-harmonic generation, and Kerr frequency comb generation. The framework is subsequently applied to a translationally symmetric waveguide to compute the evanescent coupling strength between the waveguide and a nearby microresonator, as well as the Kerr self- and cross-phase modulation terms within the resonator. Finally, this enables the derivation of a dimensionless equation governing the symmetry-breaking dynamics of two counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator, demonstrating that cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation only when the two counterpropagating modes are otherwise identical. Additionally, we offer simple, approximate expressions for all phaser space dynamics terms based on ray-optics parameters, providing excellent numerical agreement. The proposed analysis is ultimately applied to explain the conditions necessary for the emergence of phaser waves. Cross-section code is released on GitHub alongside this publication. These findings generalize the analysis originally introduced by Salamin and Courtial [arXiv:1004.0084].

Photonic phasers represent a new class of nonreciprocal devices based on the counterpropagating mode phaser (CMP) effect. This phenomenon arises from the competition between a broken symmetry due to a counterpropagating bias and a restored symmetry resulting from the Kerr nonlinearity. We outline the prerequisites for observing these phasers and describe their LIGO-like hysteresis dynamics, which can be modeled using a phaser space equation derived in prior literature [arXiv:1610:06781]. This process is initiated by the exchange energy of phaser waves, a mode-coupling effect analogous to the critical coupling of Kerr combs. Our findings indicate that the CMP effect is observable in any reflection-based resonator setup, such as those using Fabry-Perot cavities or loop resonators. To achieve the CMP conditions in such configurations, one must operate at a specific harmonic close to an anomaly—a frequency where the slope of the resonance curve becomes vertical. Adversarial Networks (GANs) to recover high-resolution turbulent velocity fields from extremely low-resolution inputs across various Reynolds numbers. The study employs a Multiscale Enhanced Super-Resolution GAN (MS-ESRGAN) for reconstruction and evaluates its performance using direct numerical simulation (DNS) data from turbulent channel flows featuring large longitudinal ribs at different Reynolds numbers. Results indicate that the model successfully and accurately reproduces high-resolution velocity fields, including velocity magnitudes and turbulent statistics, from two distinct low-resolution data levels. Furthermore, the findings demonstrate the model's capability to reconstruct velocity fields at Reynolds numbers that were not included during the training phase. Finally, the research offers insights into the characteristics of flow fields near rib surfaces and the distribution of turbulent kinetic energy within the ribbed channel, validating the model's efficacy in reconstructing complex, ribbed channel flows.

These solutions often fail to generalize effectively to new tasks beyond their training data distribution, driving interest in continual learning algorithms. Alongside algorithmic research, there is a pressing need for specialized challenge environments, rigorous experiments, and evaluation metrics. To address this gap, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a novel Unity-based first-person 3D exploration framework designed for continual reinforcement learning. Unlike worlds with randomly generated components, L2Explorer offers a systematic method for creating evolving evaluation curricula through controlled changes, complete with metrics to measure transferability, performance recovery, and data efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate that various continual learning strategies outperform standard reinforcement learning in this context, particularly when there are semantic shifts between tasks or limited in-domain training data. This paper introduces a discovery algorithm that generates Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs representing declarative processes from event streams. The algorithm identifies both the rules and non-deterministic behaviors inherent in declarative processes. These capabilities are increasingly critical for managing declarative processes, which are gaining popularity because they decouple process design from execution, offering significant flexibility. The proposed algorithm was evaluated in an empirical study involving four different processes. Furthermore, we compare our approach with existing discovery techniques, addressing how other methods handle process dynamics and non-determinism, and we outline potential application scenarios. Dynamic Condition Response graphs are declarative process models that have been extensively researched, with prior discovery algorithms focusing solely on conditional logic, thereby overlooking the temporal operators (until, next) and other non-deterministic behaviors of DCR graphs. Consequently, those earlier methods were inadequate when applied to event logs from declarative processes, particularly when processes are not fully deterministic. This study proposes a novel algorithm capable of extracting both the conditional and temporal operators, as well as other non-deterministic attributes, from event logs to construct DCR graphs. The method was benchmarked against prior discovery algorithms, and an empirical evaluation was conducted to assess discovery quality, the accuracy of handling processes over time, and the algorithm's performance efficiency. Additionally, the application of this algorithm was examined in scenarios involving process monitoring and the reverse engineering of web forms. DCR graphs provide a formal specification for declarative processes. While previous discovery algorithms were designed to extract their underlying conditional logic, this approach is often insufficient because these processes also exhibit non-deterministic attributes that were not considered in earlier work. Additionally, existing algorithms S[1] and S[2] are unable to uncover temporal operators (until and next) embedded within the process rules. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a tri-phase algorithm to discover both temporal operators and other non-deterministic attributes alongside the process's conditional logic. The proposed method was evaluated through both quantitative and qualitative approaches. Quantitative results showed that the algorithm maintains a high precision-recall balance, requiring roughly 20% fewer attributes to achieve the same discovery quality compared to state-of-the-art methods. Qualitative evaluations demonstrated that the algorithm accurately reconstructs processes that were not rediscovered by previous algorithms. ening of the star-forming main sequence (MS) at high masses. To examine how bulges influence the MS, we analyzed the NUV$-r$ color—a reliable tracer of specific star formation rate—in the central ($r<R_{50}$) versus outer regions of 6,401 local star-forming galaxies. Our results show that for galaxies with $M_{\ast}<10^{10.2}M_{\odot}$, the central NUV$-r$ is only about 0.25 magnitudes redder than the outer regions. However, above $M_{\ast}=10^{10.2}M_{\odot}$, the central NUV$-r$ becomes significantly redder than the outer regions, indicating that bulges in massive galaxies are more evolved. This trend aligns with the known increase in the bulge fraction with stellar mass. When controlling for bulge fraction, the NUV$-r$ difference between central and outer regions no longer scales with total stellar mass, suggesting that bulges do not inherently drive bulgy galaxies to higher masses on the MS. The increased quenching in bulges is partly due to a higher specific angular momentum fraction ($f_j$) among central stars compared to surface density-weighted $f_j$ in the disks. In a sample of galaxies with $10^{10.5}<M_{\ast}<10^{11.0}M_{\odot}$ and a bulge fraction $>0.1$, bulged galaxies exhibit a $\sim30\%$ higher $f_j$ in their bulges than in their disks, and this disparity correlates with the NUV$-r$ color difference. Since a lower $f_j$ is a known quenching mechanism, the angular momentum profile inherently promotes faster aging in bulges. Furthermore, other physical mechanisms, such as the outside-in migration of supermassive black holes, may also contribute to this effect. Consequently, the higher aging rate in bulges is an intrinsic property rather than a consequence of bulge fraction, and the bulge expansion scenario is unlikely to explain the main sequence evolution. The distinct aging behavior and angular momentum profiles between bulges and disks also help explain the knee in the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation observed in bulgy galaxies. These findings are based on data from the SDSS and assume no significant radial migration of stars.

The proposed system utilizes a trilingual BERT-based model trained on English, Slovene, and Croatian. The study evaluates various configurations using two-language datasets and introduces a straightforward multi-task model for sentiment classification. Assessments are carried out across single-task and multi-task experiments within both few-shot and zero-shot scenarios for Croatian and Slovene. Comparative results are drawn against current state-of-the-art models. Specifically, an LSTMs-based approach was assessed within a zero-shot context for Croatian, while a character-based method was evaluated for Slovene. Additionally, a multi-task model demonstrated superior performance when applied to both languages. In the zero-shot scenario, an F1 score of 0.79 was achieved for Croatian and 0.73 for Slovene. For the multi-task configuration, scores improved to 0.82 for Croatian and 0.75 for Slovene. The system leverages a pre-trained BERT model enhanced with a morphological tokenizer, a morphological tagger for low-resource languages, and a morphosyntactic parser. Furthermore, the study examines the effects of data volume, dropout rates, and layer counts; findings indicate that reducing layers from three to two in the BERT architecture helps avoid overfitting. Ultimately, the morphosyntactic approach proves most effective for low-resource languages, whereas the morphological method yields better results for Croatian.

However, validating this claim requires extensive, well-annotated datasets that include post-imaging severity outcomes. This paper introduces an original methodology to extract semantic features correlated with severity from patient data labeled with ICU admissions, utilizing interpretable models. The approach employs a neural network trained to identify lung pathologies to derive these features, which are subsequently analyzed using low-complexity models to mitigate overfitting and enhance interpretability. The analysis reveals that a limited number of features account for the majority of variance between patients who develop severe symptoms. When applied to a larger, unrelated dataset containing pathology-related clinical notes, the method demonstrated the ability to select images representing learned features, potentially mapping common anatomical locations within the lung. Beyond confirming separability among patients destined for severe outcomes, the proposed statistical approach underscores the significance of features associated with ICU admission that were previously only qualitatively described. Despite handling limited data, the methodology incorporates state-of-the-art lung segmentation and low-complexity modeling to prevent overfitting. The code for the methodology and experiments is publicly available.

Abstract elements are fundamental, widely applicable components of human thought, yet current AI systems lack mechanisms to both discover and represent them. We utilize a generative approach to automatically identify abstract elements embedded within diverse clinical notes regarding a specific disease. By employing a model with limited capacity, we prevent overfitting and enable the system to propose candidate abstract elements. Subsequently, we leverage an interpretable model to verify that these elements are indeed represented within the notes. The resulting proposed abstract elements are concise, semantically meaningful, and align with clinical expertise. Furthermore, our method is scalable, making it suitable for exploration across large datasets. Unlike prior methods, this scalable approach yields a library of abstract elements that can be combined to explain variations in machine learning model predictions. Although developed for clinical text, the methodology is modality-agnostic and can be adapted to apply to other data types, such as images or signals.

To address this, we developed a scalable, interpretable framework that facilitates the discovery of informative, abstract features. p(\mathcal{C}) \to sSet(\mathcal{C})$, defined for simplicial groups within a category $\mathcal{C}$ possessing finite products, can be elevated to a monad on $sGrp(\mathcal{C})$. This finding generalizes to simplicial algebras associated with any Lawvere theory that includes the theory of groups. Furthermore, we establish that the universal bundle functor preserves homotopy limits under specific conditions. These conditions are characterized by the vanishing of certain maps between derived mapping stacks of the base category $\mathcal{C}$. We provide an explicit formula for the derived limit of a composite functor involving these maps and verify the necessary axioms for this construction to function as a homotopy limit. The main theorem is applied to demonstrate that $W$ satisfies the homotopy anti-Severi condition, thereby yielding a result by step (anti)6-homotopy limits. Additionally, we explore the connection between our approach and the standard construction of universal bundles, analyzing the relationship between these two methods through an explicit comparison morphism. These investigations are conducted within the broader context of the general functor $W: sAlg(\mathcal{C}) \to sSet(\mathcal{C})$. The primary innovation of this paper lies in utilizing a bar resolution of a simplicial object in $\mathcal{C}$ to define the derived limit, which is then employed to formulate the condition for $W$ preserving homotopy limits. This contrasts with the conventional approach, which typically relies on the assumption that $\mathcal{C}$ has homotopy limit. We also examine the fundamental properties of this derived limit and illustrate its application in proving the preservation of specific homotopy limits by $W$. The fundamental group of the total space of the universal bundle is calculated, and its long exact sequence of homotopy groups is explicitly described. Finally, we determine the Euler characteristic of the total space and explore its relation to the homology of the base space's geometric realization via a natural transformation. These findings extend and offer an alternative perspective on established results by Aracil, Bredon, and Whitehead concerning the universal bundle functor for simplicial groups. Additionally, we examine the analogous situation for the universal principal bundle functor for simplicial Lie groups. {\\em Keywords:} universal bundle functor, universal principal bundle, simplicial group, simplicial algebra, Bar resolution, homotopy limit, (anti)-6-homotopy limit, homotopy

positive rate in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). We note that training is hindered by a skewed relationship profile, where a small subset of predicates accounts for the majority of proposals and positive training examples, a phenomenon we term the Long-Tail Problem. To address this, we introduce a simple, cost-effective solution utilizing a two-stage approach with an external repository for rare predicates. To further investigate false positive origins, we propose utilizing a rarity-based filter to eliminate common-background noise. This filter leverages the low frequency of true training examples for each predicate to flag high-confidence false positives. We validate these findings through additional experiments and visualizations, and we provide a GitHub link to the proposed solution. Our solution achieves a 10% improvement in mAP for rare predicates compared to the original VRD approach and requires only 25% more time for training and inference. We also present visual evidence that the Long-Tail Problem is a primary source of false positives, filter out high-confidence false positives, and demonstrate improved mean-average precision across all buckets of frequent and rare predicates. Furthermore, by showing that the problem's severity correlates with scene complexity, we suggest adapting the threshold based on detected object counts. Finally, we illustrate the practical utility of VRD in filtering spammed action recognition predictions. Our code and video demonstrations confirm these contributions. We hope our visual analysis aids researchers in addressing the Long-Tail Problem and using VRD to filter common-background noise to improve action recognition. Please refer to our acceptance track submission for a video version of this presentation. Video demos are available at this link.

imeter observations of three massive ($>10^{11}\,\rm M_{\odot}$), highly star-forming galaxies located in the core of the RO-1001 group at redshift $z=2.91$. Each galaxy features compact, kiloparsec-scale starburst cores with characteristics indicative of forming bulges, situated within extended, massive stellar disks. Notably, these disks are both distinctly quiescent and severely asymmetric. This configuration suggests that "outside-in" quenching is actively occurring in these group members. We propose a scenario where the significant mass asymmetry in the disks (varying by factors of 1.6 to over 3), likely induced by accreted gas and clumps, suppresses star formation in the outer regions while channeling gas toward the nuclei to fuel central starbursts. The asymmetric side of the disks indicates the impact site of accretion streams, with nearby dust and stellar components directly tracing the inflow direction. Interactions with these accreted clumps, viewed as minor mergers, align the major axes of the three galaxies with external Lyman-$\alpha$-emitting feeding filaments. These findings offer the first observational proof of how cold accretion streams influence galaxy formation and evolution. Currently, this process manifests as the rapid assembly of bulges driven by accretion, while maintaining massive, quiescent, and highly asymmetric disks. Direct detections of associated accretion streams are still needed to fully validate this model. These asymmetric massive galaxies at $z\sim3$ may serve as the precursors to the $z<1$ $L_*$ galaxies that currently possess minor-axis-oriented spurs, as indicated by their progenitor properties.

Bolivia (5250 m a.s.l.) and Mexico (4600 m a.s.l.) detected a notable event on November 7, 2004, linked to an X2.0-class solar flare. Data from our records, alongside observations from GOES 11 and SOHO satellites, indicate that electrons and protons—potential byproducts of neutron decay—were present. While solar neutron decay protons (sndp) were previously detected aboard the ISEE3 satellite on June 3, 1982, and by ground-level instruments in Goose Bay and Deep River on October 19, 1989, this marks the second instance of such evidence being recorded directly on Earth's surface. Our detectors in Bolivia and Mexico offer the most direct detection method, as they are positioned nearly 90 degrees in longitude from the sun during solar conjunction, ensuring that our background-free signals were not contaminated by beam halo particles from the Voyager1 probe. These sndp arrived approximately three hours after the neutron explosion and persisted for three hours, driving a significant (>20%) count rate enhancement three days after the neutron event. We propose that these count rates resulted from a flood of solar protons trapped in the radiation belts following a lack of magnetospheric damping oscillations post-solar conjunction. This mechanism was also observed following an X2.6 flare on September 10, 2017. Furthermore, the delays in count rate enhancement following the two largest X-class flares of 2012 and 2017 suggest that the mechanism involves not only a failure to dampen geomagnetic oscillations immediately after conjunction but potentially other factors, such as the gradual accumulation of radiation from proton precipitation along the magnetopause. Ultimately, sndp can be expected to follow all future X-class and higher solar flares, particularly when the sun is near conjunction. These findings were supported by analyses of time-of-flight, count rate profiles, and neutron explosion characteristics. Our results demonstrate that modern neutrino detectors can serve as effective instruments for space physics by detecting solar neutron decay protons. Neutrino detectors feature large surface areas, excellent count rate resolution, and superior low-energy thresholds, allowing them to resolve count rate enhancement mechanisms that satellite-based narrow-beam instruments often miss. Additionally, the advanced electronics within these detectors enable the precise determination of time-of-flight for trapped radiation, facilitating a deeper understanding of the physics governing these phenomena. Neutrino detectors will continue to provide high-resolution

otonic radial rotation profile in a low-mass, low-luminosity giant star. While low- and intermediate-mass stars typically exhibit rigid rotation on the main sequence, stellar evolution into the giant phase—characterized by core contraction and envelope expansion—generally predicts a profile with a rapidly rotating core and a slower envelope and surface. KIC 9267654, however, displays a surface rotation rate exceeding that of its bulk envelope, contradicting standard angular momentum conservation expectations. We enhance the spectroscopic constraints on the surface rotation, confirm that pulsation frequencies align with previously determined global angular momentum characteristics, and outline prospects for future envelope rotation measurements using *PLATO*. Furthermore, we highlight that the unexpectedly high angular momentum of KIC 9267654 cannot be accounted for by standard stellar evolution models without envelope magnetic braking. These findings underscore the significance of KIC 9267654 as a target for precise angular momentum tracing with the PLATO mission, potentially offering insights into the physics driving this anomalous angular momentum buildup. Additionally, we suggest that similar analysis of asteroseismic data from $\delta$ Scuti and slow rotors could reveal comparable, hitherto unappreciated angular momentum challenges in that group. KIC 9267654 was previously identified by Juntara et al. (2018). (original version contains 10 figures and 3 tables).

The analysis is restricted to odd functions, a constraint imposed to manage the periodic nature of the term $Hu$ at the boundaries. Throughout the paper, lengthy and intricate calculations are concentrated in the appendices.
