In this paper, we extend GCMs to multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays (GCA) and introduce new construction methods for GCA pairs and quads. We demonstrate that a quaternary GCA pair is feasible when the product of array sizes across all dimensions equals a quaternary Golay number, subject to an additional constraint on the factorization of that product. Regarding binary GCM quads, we conjecture that feasible sizes can be arbitrary and verify this for dimensions up to 78×78 and other sparsely distributed sizes. OmniCode utilizes multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays to design low-complexity, widebeam, and omnidirectional codes for both single-and multi-user multi-antenna transmission scenarios. This achievement is verified through simulations using a 5G NR physical layer air interface simulator.

While phosphorus dopants in silicon can be positioned with atomic precision to explore these competing regimes, they typically rely on crystal band symmetry-based wavefunctions that are intrinsically sensitive to tunneling effects. This study directly visualizes lattice-aperiodic valley interference between coupled silicon atoms using scanning tunneling microscopy. Our atomistic analysis reveals how envelope anisotropy, valley interference, and dopant positioning influence the Heisenberg spin exchange interaction. Although graph neural networks (GNNs) offer a valuable relational inductive bias for modeling these systems, research into their ability to generalize to new instances within the same system type remains limited. In this study, we trained GNNs to learn time series data from a specific nonlinear dynamical system known as the belief propagation algorithm. Our analysis revealed that the learned representations and model components have simple, interpretable representations with a strong, clear bias toward the relational structure of the target system. By systematically exploring the parameter space of the trained models, we identified a linear subspace that is shared across different instances of the dynamical system. This finding suggests a simple, linearly separable representation for this class of dynamical systems. Ultimately, we developed a novel generator network that leverages this explicit bias to predict a "mean" representation for new instances of systems it has only observed in part. Evaluations on both synthetic and real-world data (including earthquake recurrence and animal foraging) confirm the generalizability, interpretability, and cost-effectiveness of our approach, offering a promising foundation for future work in this domain.

Earthquake recurrence can be modeled as a self-organized criticality process, where the spatial distribution of past quakes heavily influences future ones. We developed a neural network capable of generalizing to unseen geographic locations and times by utilizing spatial coordinates as its sole input, aside from the historical sequence of magnitudes. This generalization is achieved by embedding spatial coordinates into a dedicated embedding layer, which provides a data-efficient representation of location that captures the underlying physics of the problem. The network's design and our analysis consistently align with the principles of the Bayesian Perceptron, even when processing real-world data. Our results indicate that the perceptual boundary for generalizing earthquake recurrence is determined by the Earth's curvature, a result that holds true regardless of the specific belief function, prior distribution, or other model hyperparameters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this generalization capability is not limited to natural phenomena, as it can be applied to any recurrent system that can be represented as a graph.

Ultimately, this method demonstrates that high-quality synthetic data can be created using generative models and can effectively enhance the accuracy of ROI segmentation.

To mitigate this, GP 2 introduces rooted rules that, provided mild conditions are met, allow for constant-time matching. Recently, we enhanced Bak's GP 2-to-C compiler with several modifications to accelerate graph programs. This represents the latest iteration in a series of efforts to develop a high-performance GP 2-to-C compiler, following prior work that accelerated specific analysis tasks [10,11], which eventually culminated in a full evaluation using a suite of GP 2 programs [1]. These findings indicate that modern hardware can execute graph programs efficiently when employing appropriate data structures and a fast-to-build compiler. To support researchers aiming to create even faster graph programs on current hardware, we offer practical guidelines derived from our performance study. This is achievable because our profiling results reveal that CPU cache effects dominate overall execution time. In summary, this paper presents GP 2's background, details the features of our new, fast compiler, and explores both caloric and performance profiles to achieve substantial speedups for graph programs on modern systems.

Given the recent surge in interest toward contrastive learning as a prominent self-supervised technique, this study introduces a unified framework grounded in a novel perspective of contrastive learning (CL), applicable to both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework initially establishes two distinct CL graphs to precisely define positive and negative pairs, followed by the determination of a projection matrix through the minimization of a contrastive loss function. Furthermore, the approach integrates both similar and dissimilar samples to harmonize unsupervised and supervised extraction processes. Specifically, the study proposes three methodologies: an unsupervised contrastive learning approach, along with two distinct supervised contrastive learning methods. Extensive numerical experiments conducted across five real-world datasets confirm that the proposed framework outperforms existing methods. Additionally, the findings from these experiments offer insights into the innovative contrastive learning framework introduced in this paper.

Deep learning techniques have achieved significant success in various applications, yet their heavy computational costs and data-specific nature often limit their ability to generalize when new information arises. To overcome these limitations, we introduced the Updateable Neural Atoms framework in earlier work, which employs an additive model to represent large neural networks. This model allows most components to be pre-trained and shared, while replacing heavily parameterized sub-networks with efficiently trained neural atoms that capture unique local features of specific data domains. These atoms can be readily re-trained when new data becomes available. In this follow-up study, we explore the application of the Additive Neural Atom model in transfer learning. Our results demonstrate that this approach not only matches the performance of full-network training but also exceeds that of current state-of-the-art methods. By combining updateable neural atoms with an additional mechanism for incorporating external knowledge, we developed the Updateable Neural Atom Network (UNANet). UNANet utilizes shared backbone networks and enhances performance through the addition of task-specific neural atoms. These atoms are lightweight, easy to train, and highly adaptable to new tasks. Experimental evaluations on benchmark datasets for self-expression completion and cross-domain object detection show that UNANet outperforms state-of-the-art approaches. We view this study as a complementary extension to our previous research, collectively illustrating the versatility of the neural atom concept in adapting large networks for updateable and transferable capabilities. This work extends the UNANet framework, offering users a practical solution for maintaining high-performance predictive models in dynamic, real-world scenarios.

This research advances the classification initiative launched by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by demonstrating that the star normal quotient twisted wreath category encompasses infinitely many such graphs. Furthermore, we provide a complete characterization of the vertex orbit actions under this quasiprimitive framework. The corresponding graphs and their automorphism groups are defined as follows: let $X(p,n)$ denote the lexicographic product $K_{2p} \square^n$ with its 1-factorizations edge-transitively paired via a sequence of symmetric swap maps, where $p = 2^{n-1}3$ and $n \geq 2$; the graph $X(p,n)$ admits a quasiprimitive action on one vertex orbit, with its full 1-factorization being edge-transitive, governed by the twisted wreath group $S_{2p} \bowtie n$. Additionally, $X(5,3)$ is introduced as a new example, as its automorphism group is not 2-transitive on vertices, a property not covered by the existing literature. We fully describe the orbit, arc, and suborbit structures for both $X(p,n)$ and $X(5,3)$, along with their respective automorphism groups. These findings indicate that the families $X(p,n)$ and $X(5,3)$ exhibit a high degree of symmetry, as their 1-factorizations are edge-transitive and their edge swap constructions are locally edge-transitive. The construction of $X(p,n)$ is general and potentially widely applicable. We confirm that the families $X(p,n)$ and $X(5,3)$ are arc transitive, noting however that their full automorphism groups are not so. Our work thus contributes to the ongoing effort of classifying all arc transitive graphs that are locally arc transitive and possess a quasiprimitive automorphism group on a vertex orbit.

Although Group Lasso is a recognized efficient method for selecting both continuous and categorical variables, it often yields distinct estimates for each level of a selected factor, resulting in non-sparse fitted models that are hard to interpret. To achieve sparsity with Group Lasso, we propose a two-step approach: first, use Group Lasso to reduce data dimensionality; second, select the final model by applying an information criterion to a restricted set of models generated by clustering the levels of individual factors. This study introduces a technique to embed structured knowledge into LLMs by directly training T5 models on factual triples extracted from knowledge graphs. When applied to the smaller WikiMovies dataset, our method achieved a threefold increase in exact match scores on the MetaQA task relative to the T5 baseline. A key benefit of this approach is that it eliminates the need for aligning knowledge graphs with text corpora during data preparation, rendering it especially advantageous for industry-scale knowledge graphs. To facilitate this, we provide access to a structured knowledge-base-enhanced T5 model trained on Wikidata facts and offer instructions for replicable training on WikiMovies. To our knowledge, this is the first method to exhibit such significant knowledge acquisition in a transfer learning setting. Beyond its practical success, our findings contradict prior research indicating that T5 fails to absorb knowledge from large knowledge bases within pretraining data. By directly training on factual triples, we highlight the importance of textual variations when generating knowledge for modern LLMs and demonstrate that large T5 models can efficiently learn these facts. By dividing long sequences into smaller segments and utilizing dual-path recurrent units, the DPRNN effectively integrates local and global contextual features. Building on this, we propose the Convoluted Dual-Path RNN (CDPRNN), which incorporates a convolution module to extract local features within the dual-path RNN. ### 1. Introduction
Since Belfelt first demonstrated in the frequency domain that a single feedforward neural network could learn to separate a noisy mixture of two sources, time-domain methods have also proven effective for this task. Various networks, including NCRF++ , CRNN , and Concolinear RNNs , have achieved state-of-the-art results. Although the DPRNN is a relatively recent and efficient architecture that has yielded promising outcomes, its performance can still be enhanced. The primary goal of this paper is to introduce a novel model capable of processing long sequences for time-domain speech separation.

This study examines the connection between the observable shadow radius and the first-order phase transition of non-linear charged AdS black holes within the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. The analysis reveals that, under specific conditions, the shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature exhibit qualitative differences when treated as functions of the charge parameter across various non-linear electromagnetic field strengths. Furthermore, when the electric field derives from a U(1) gauge field, we demonstrate that the shadow radius remains unchanged whether the boundary condition is identified or Dirichlet, provided the temperature is defined via the horizon radius. However, under non-abelian strong coupling conditions, the shadow radius becomes dependent on the boundary condition. These findings indicate that, for an AdS space with a U(1) gauge field, the boundary condition cannot remain fixed across different bulk theories if the shadow radius is used as a probe for thermodynamic phase transitions. Beyond the shadow radius, we also explore other physical quantities, such as the entropy and heat capacity, to gain further insights into the system's phase transitions. Regarding the phase transition defined by the shadow radius, we find that the critical state equation is $Pv+c=0$, with $c$ representing an unknown constant that varies based on the non-linear electromagnetic field parameter; this contrasts with AdS black holes under the Dirichlet boundary condition, where $c=-1$. Ultimately, this transition differs from the Hawking-Page transition and cannot be detected using only the boundary metric. Our results suggest that the shadow radius serves as a powerful tool for probing thermodynamic phase transitions, particularly in regimes where the non-linear charged AdS black hole system approaches its critical point. These findings offer significant insights into the thermodynamics of AdS black holes under non-abelian strong coupling. However, these conclusions are strictly valid only when the AdS curvature radius is directly proportional to the thermal radius. We present our principal results in this paper and will explore additional physical quantities related to the non-linear charged AdS black hole system in our upcoming work.

While numerous reconstruction methods exist—from conventional protocols to machine learning approaches—no single universal technique currently allows for extracting the Wigner function from the optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that nonclassical phenomena, including entanglement variations during dynamical evolution and the emergence of quantum synchronization, manifest as qualitative shifts within the optical tomograms themselves. Consequently, explicit state reconstruction is unnecessary to detect these effects. Because optical tomograms readily encode quantum entangled states, we propose two specific scenarios where exact reconstruction is dispensable: detecting (i) amplitude-squeezed entangled states within a NOON state family and (ii) the quantum synchronization between two modes of the radiation field. Furthermore, we show that even the quantum entropy of the radiation field's state can be estimated without knowing the exact state, relying only on sample sizes and a specific confidence level. Collectively, these scenarios represent novel examples where quantum state reconstruction is not required, as the necessary physical information is already fully contained within the optical tomogram. The proposed strategies are generic and can be adapted to reconstruct the density operator of any other bosonic system, such as atomic ensembles, mechanical resonators, or photonic networks. The absence of post-selection enhances the efficiency of the proposed NOON state analysis, making it significantly more practical than existing spectral or homodyne detection-based reconstruction methods. Consequently, the experimental cost for state reconstruction reduces to generating optical tomograms, which is frequently unavoidable in other contexts. The fundamental mathematics and numerical simulations validating this conclusion are provided in the Supplemental Material [Suppl. Mater. Quantum Sci. Quantum mechanics fundamentally relies on the linearity of Hilbert spaces. In contrast, widely used computational frameworks, including tensor networks, are inherently non-linear. This discrepancy creates a paradox when attempting to formulate physical theories based solely on tensor network formalisms. While recent advances have established rigorous conditions for PEPOs to represent thermal states and time evolution, these solutions generally demand a bond dimension scaling with system size. We instead develop estimates that depend exclusively on temperature or time. Although these new bounds may be conservative, they enable the study of large systems at low temperatures or short durations. Additionally, quantum field theory emerges naturally from the translation invariance of these PEPOs.

Observables in condensed matter physics are characterized by how quickly correlations between local quantities decay with distance. This connection to dynamical critical exponent $z$ is not merely qualitative; it governs the difficulty of simulating these systems via tensor network methods. Although recent methodological improvements have lowered the temperature scaling of the bond dimension $D$ needed to compute correlation functions, such approaches often remain dependent on system size $N$. We introduce a formalism where $D$ scales with temperature rather than $N$, yielding the first numerical calculation of dynamic critical exponents using PEPOs. These new techniques allow us to determine $z$ directly from the decay of temporal correlations in a quantum critically thermalized state, or from the decay of correlations post-quench, using a bond dimension scaling as $t^z$ or $\beta^z$, respectively. We validate these findings with numerical results for the transverse field Ising model and the quantum Heisenberg model.

### 1 Introduction

Deep learning has driven significant advances in fields like computer vision, natural language processing, and speech recognition. These applications depend on large-scale models trained with extensive data and computational resources. Consequently, deploying such heavy-capacity networks in resource-limited environments remains a major hurdle. Knowledge distillation (KD) offers an efficient solution by enabling a small student network to learn from a sophisticated teacher model with minimal training data.

In standard white-box KD, a student approximates the teacher's internal representations or output probabilities, requiring access to training data and the teacher's parameters. However, in many practical cases, accessing these internal parameters or even the original training data is unfeasible due to privacy, security, or storage issues. Moreover, some deployed models operate as decision-based black-box systems, leaking only class labels during queries. In such settings, white-box KD becomes inapplicable.

To overcome these limitations, we propose two decision-based black-box KD strategies that only require the teacher's class labels as input. The first method generates soft labels by leveraging the robustness of training samples against the teacher's decision boundaries. The second method creates a transfer set using pseudo-samples and soft labels derived from the teacher's decision boundaries. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a new framework named Co-Imitation Learning (CoIL), which utilizes an agent's own historical successful experiences rather than relying on external experts. Likelihood Estimation (MLE) pre-training is a flexible approach for boosting Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Nevertheless, recent studies suggest that RL's benefits in NMT largely stem from reinforcing tokens that were already highly probable during pre-training. We propose that the extensive action space is a primary barrier to RL's efficacy in machine translation and validate this hypothesis through two experimental series. First, we observe that shrinking the vocabulary size enhances RL performance. Second, we demonstrate that effectively lowering the action space dimensionality without altering the vocabulary also leads to significant gains, as this method avoids common vanishing gradient issues within the translator's encoding layers. Consequently, we offer a practical guideline for deploying RL in NMT and confirm with additional analyses that using a sequence-level reward function, such as COMET, further amplifies RL's impact. Overall, our findings indicate that RL is particularly valuable for preserving the quality and diversity of a model's baseline outputs, a capability that becomes harder to achieve with larger models that possess higher inherent quality and diversity. Thus, RL should be considered when developing high-quality MMT systems, even those exceeding 1 billion parameters. Our codebase is available at https://github.com/maynes/mt-rl-analysis.

Machine translation evaluates a language model's capacity to predict a cross-lingual sequence of words given a source sentence. While large-scale training enhances a model's language modeling skills, it often leads to over-translation, resulting in mother-tongue like outputs. We introduce a novel multi-objective reinforcement learning (RL) framework for machine translation that addresses this issue. This framework utilizes a reward model trained on source-language text to constrain mono-lingual over-translation. To handle the multiple reward signals, we employ an attention-based mechanism to dynamically select distributions over actions. Experimental results on three Mandarin English translation datasets (NMTCorpus, WMT19, and a low-resource set) show that our method surpasses existing cross-lingual reward RL approaches. Specifically, compared to the strongest baseline, our method achieves a +0.44 BLEU point increase, a +2.46 point improvement in COMET, and a +3.04 point gain in Google Translate Score on the NMTCorpus dataset.

This study experimentally investigates time-discrete, periodically driven dynamics in a single photon coupled to an environment. Constructed as Wronskians of standard Hermite polynomials, these polynomials are significant in mathematical physics, random matrix theory, and one-dimensional supersymmetric (SUSY) quantum mechanics. Characterized by quadratic behavior at infinity, these potentials exhibit localized oscillations near the origin. We establish an explicit criterion for the non-singularity of the associated potentials and estimate their localization range based on polynomial indices and the distribution of their complex zeros. Our findings reveal that non-singular 1D SUSY quantum potentials arise from dressing the harmonic oscillator using polynomial Heisenberg algebra ladder operators. Consequently, all generalized Hermite polynomials are generated through the appropriate periodic closure of this algebra, yielding rational solutions to the Painlevé IV equation. Finally, we examine the structure of the discrete spectrum for these Schrödinger operators and its relationship to the monodromy-free condition. This analysis extends to the continuous spectrum, connecting the problem to the classical stability of the periodic Painlevé IV scission base on the complex plane. These results are illustrated with specific examples.

By applying a phase space reconstruction method, we confirm deterministic chaotic dynamics through the identification of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent within a specific range of traction speeds. These findings are interpreted using a model that underscores the deterministic nature of acoustic emissions by linking them to stick-slip dynamics. This approach provides an alternative to optical methods for studying material fracture and crosslinking in noisy experimental setups. The procedure detailed herein is entirely non-invasive, can be implemented with standard acoustic sensors, and involves complex data analysis only at the post-processing stage. The study's key contribution lies in utilizing a reconstructed low-dimensional phase space (attractors) to prove the deterministic and chaotic nature of the noise-free acoustic emission signals. By employing the Thermofield Dynamics formalism to account for temperature and spatial compactification, the analysis calculates corrections arising from this non-abelian term to the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law, as well as to the Casimir energy and pressure at both zero and finite temperatures. These calculations are based on the quadratic Lagrangian approximation, yielding terms proportional to the square of the aether parameters. The study also explores the case where the pure gauge field is subjected to a uniform electric field. The findings suggest that, at sufficiently high temperatures, the term linked to Lorentz symmetry breaking causes the system to enter a confining phase, even in the absence of interactions with an external world. Consequently, the slight discrepancy between the Casimir energy at finite temperature and its zero-temperature limit serves as a robust indicator of Lorentz symmetry breaking, provided the temperature is not excessively low. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that at zero temperature, the presence of the aether term can induce the emergence of a non-zero Casimir energy, implying that the Yang-Mills-aether term acts as a source of Casimir energy. These conclusions are derived assuming periodic boundary conditions for the aether term itself. However, if the boundary conditions are changed to Dirichlet, the term responsible for triggering the transition to the confining phase at high temperatures disappears. This is because, under Dirichlet conditions, the aether term reduces to a constant at any temperature, causing the phase transition temperature to vanish. This effect is directly attributable to the non-abelian nature of the term $\eta_{\mu\nu}W^{\nu\lambda}W^{ }_{\lambda}$. Ultimately, the research highlights that the Casimir energy at finite temperature can function as a diagnostic tool for the presence of the Yang-Mills-aether term, even when the energy magnitude is small. Ultimately, various physical scenarios involving Yang-Mills theory with Lorentz symmetry violation are identified as promising areas for future investigation.

The study derives a simplified expression for this liquidity function and establishes bounds for both delta and its rate of change with respect to the option's delta. The model also supports the assessment of the liquidity efficiency of exchanges and market makers. Furthermore, the proposed model is general enough to be utilized for other financial derivatives. By validating models on other markets, researchers can advance understanding of trader behavior and liquidity dynamics. Consequently, this work provides regulators with tools to monitor market maker efficiency and the liquidity of individual ticks. To achieve this, we employ a dataset comprising 60 seconds of high-frequency data from the CBOE Cals option traded on the CBOT VIX future. We formulate the liquidity costing problem as follows: Let $C(t,K)$ represent the price of a European call option with strike price $K$ at time $t$, where $0\leq t\leq T$ and $T$ is the option's expiration. Let $\Delta C(t,K) = \frac{\partial C}{\partial S_t}$ denote the option's delta. The proposed liquidity costing model is defined by the equation: $$cost = \int_{K_{min}}^{K_{max}} \left| \Delta C(T-a,K) \right|^{1+\frac{1}{2.5}\sin \left( \frac{K}{a \times 0.05} \right)} dK.$$ This formulation captures the intricate nature of option liquidity, which varies over time and across different strikes, thereby supporting trading strategies that account for these factors. By analyzing data from other markets, researchers can gain insights into trading dynamics and liquidity pricing. We construct a dynamic framework for distributing such opportunities within a society characterized by mobility bottlenecks, where optimal allocation involves balancing the immediate benefits to the current generation against the potential to uplift future generations' socioeconomic composition. Our analysis demonstrates that optimal allocations emerge from continuous optimization problems spanning multiple generations, revealing that these solutions often prioritize individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds over slightly more successful high-status peers—a form of affirmative action that arises organically from the pursuit of payoff maximization. Furthermore, we examine how model parameters influence whether this affirmative action is temporary or persistent, and we explore extensions incorporating more complex mechanisms governing transitions between socioeconomic levels. This research underscores how dynamic access models highlight access as a potent tool for enhancing mobility, offers insights into designing such systems, and provides actionable guidance for policymakers. Access to education serves as a mechanism through which individuals can overcome inherited socioeconomic disadvantages; when such access is limited, the benefit of selecting high-potential individuals outweighs promoting generational mobility. Conversely, when individual access payoffs are low and moderate gains can significantly elevate a person's status, optimal allocation prioritizes generating a more capable next generation over maximizing current payoffs, making affirmative action based on ancestry endogenous and persistent. Dynamic access models also reveal that while these mechanisms can persist, their intensity may fluctuate over time, and factors influencing the model parameters often determine the underlying mechanisms driving persistent affirmative action.

Access to education represents a mechanism that can facilitate mobility, allowing individuals to surpass the standing of their parents. We demonstrate that this approach yields an affirmative action mechanism that selects applicants with the highest payoffs, yet such mechanisms are contingent upon specific environmental conditions. Furthermore, we introduce a persistent "canonical" mechanism derived from a periodic optimization problem, which chooses individuals with the second-highest payoffs. These findings are based on a dynamic priority rule governing university access that prioritizes generations with the highest socioeconomic standing. This ordering mechanism relies on a bottleneck effect, assuming that an individual can only improve their status relative to their parents up to a certain threshold, beyond which they assume the highest possible standing. Large Hadron Collider (LHC) implemented a novel rapid luminosity separation technique known as "Emittance Scans." These scans were executed systematically during every fill featuring full-intensity beams under physics production conditions at the Interaction Point (IP) of the Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) experiment. This method enables the determination of emittance by gradually changing the skew quadrupole settings in one of the two colliding beams. By analyzing both the collision geometry and a series of luminosity-based metrics, the longitudinal emittance can be derived from the expected Gaussian distribution of the interaction point along the beamline. Given that transverse emittances are directly linked to both the geometric and luminosity parameters of the colliding beams, the fast emittance scan technique serves as a powerful instrument for quickly and precisely measuring total emittances throughout the entire LHC injection chain. At LHC-IP8, verified with data from 2015, this method yielded a 2.3% precision in prompt emittance measurements over a 2016 LHC fill cycle, surpassing the 10% precision previously attainable through other methods across the same cycle. Furthermore, by leveraging the high-statistics proton-proton collision data acquired via emittance scans at LHC-I8, researchers can reconstruct the complete LHC injection process remotely using the Statistical Emittance Reconstruction (SER) technique. This reconstructed data can then be employed to monitor emittance trends over extended periods, such as an entire year at the LHC, using small, strategically selected data samples from fills at high-luminosity IP11 or from dedicated emittance scan fills. Consequently, fast emittance scans offer a robust method for enhancing the reliability of Physics Long Term Emittance Studies (PLTES). These studies can utilize small data samples extracted throughout the entire LHC fill cycle to track the evolution of beam emittances from injection to dump, providing valuable insights for optimizing future LHC operations. The VERIFICATION at LHC-I8 and the application of SER following these scans demonstrate that modern data-recording and analysis capabilities, combined with the fast emittance scan method, can replace older single epunch telemetry systems for gathering LHC injection data. This combination will significantly enhance the study of LHC injection chain reliability in upcoming installations. Keywords: LHC, CERN, proton-proton collisions, beam emittance, emittance scan, interaction point, IP8, data analysis, SER, reliability, injection chain, PLTES.

background (CMB) serves as a fundamental probe in physical cosmology. Due to the faintness of this signal, researchers have developed increasingly sophisticated and sensitive experiments that observe the sky across multiple frequencies using thousands of polarization-sensitive detectors. However, the high sensitivity of these instruments means that instrumental systematic effects can become the primary obstacle to fully exploiting their data. This paper introduces s4cmb (Systematics for CMB), a Python package designed to simulate realistic instrumental instrumental effects for polarized CBs. The package begins by outlining the rigorous data processing pipeline required to derive precise cosmological parameters from current and future observations. It demonstrates how to simulate instrumental systematics for a simulated Delphini-type detector array, covering the entire pipeline from raw data to a final map. The s4cmb package is open-source, fostering collaboration among observers, analysts, and theorists to systematically investigate instrumental issues in real CB observations by leveraging their high sensitivity and extensive data volumes. By doing so, the package aims to establish a robust data processing framework that not only identifies and constrains instrumental systematics to unlock the full scientific potential of modern CB observations but also accurately incorporate realistic instrument models into statistical analyses for primary CB signals. The package name s4cmb is a pun on the Australian Aboriginal song "S4men," created to humorously address the challenge of detecting tiny thermal fluctuations from the earliest universe while grappling with complex instrumental systematic effects. The s4cmb package is open source and available at https://github.com/HiroyaTada/s4cmb. Tada et al. (2021) provide further details on the package. K. Menger explored the concept of an abstract angle function, defining it broadly for metric and semi-metric spaces. He also formulated two challenges regarding the conformal embeddability of spaces equipped with an angle function into Euclidean spaces. Although these problems garnered attention later, solutions were limited to specific instances of metric spaces. This article updates the definition of the angle function to accommodate a broader class of spaces characterized by a betweenness relation, which we consider a more natural framework. Within this generalized setting, we resolve both problems originally posed by Menger. First, we provide a revised definition of the angle function that subsumes every betweenness space. Second, we demonstrate that any betweenness space fulfilling a slightly strengthened version of the axioms can isomorphically embed into Euclidean space as a convex set. These results extend previous findings by K. Korczak. The proof strategy relies on developing a betweenness-relational counterpart to the conformal mapping constructed in the work of Riemann and Weierstrass. We believe this application of classical geometry holds significant potential for addressing open problems in the theory of betweenness spaces. To support these claims, we include numerous illustrations and betweenness-relational versions of key theorems from differential and conformal geometerysupporting our assertion that this classical geometric approach is optimal for solving problems in betweenness space theory. Notably, our proof utilizes a recent result by V. Dubecoq on the differentiability of betweenness functions in Hilbert spaces. However, we offer a streamlined demonstration of this result, rendering it applicable to both Hilbert and Banach spaces. To achieve this, we introduced a novel betweenness-relational version of the logarithmic conformal map found in literature. Furthermore, we establish a new betweenness-relational intermediate value theorem, which, alongside a Hahn-type betweenness-relational theorem by G. Buskes and R. Nanbu, is essential for proving the conformal nature of the mapping between a deep ocean floor model and a 2D map, as well as for establishing the theorem by Dubecoq. These contributions advance the research of A. Levenshtein and others. The findings present betweenness-relational calculus as a viable alternative to its differential counterpart for addressing problems in conformal geometry. We conclude by outlining several interesting directions for future work. The main results are summarized in Papers A and B. Although these schemes have operated for over a century, their internal dynamics and community structures have remained unstudied due to the opaque nature of participant transactions. This paper offers an empirical investigation of Forsage, a pyramid scheme executed via a smart contract that became one of Ethereum's most resource-intensive applications at its peak. Unlike traditional schemes, Forsage's bytecode and transaction history are fully visible on the blockchain, allowing us to leverage this transparency to examine its operational mechanics, impact on users, and development over time. We measured the multi-million-dollar profits earned by top-level participants alongside the losses suffered by the vast majority of users (approximately 88%). By analyzing the code both manually and through a custom-built transaction simulator, we revealed the scheme's intricate mechanisms. Furthermore, by examining promotional videos and social media activity, we demonstrated how promoters utilized the distinctive capabilities of smart contracts to deceive users with misleading claims of trust and profitability, and how the scheme's activity was concentrated within specific national communities. By utilizing a transaction simulator, we constructed a comprehensive dataset of user outcomes, revealing the scheme's evolving tactics and how its multi-phase structure influenced participation and results. Our findings indicate that pyramid schemes can harness the power of smart contracts and the blockchain while retaining all their deceptive characteristics. The pyramid's architecture ensured that the majority of users (88%) suffered significant losses, while the top 10% of participants generated the overwhelming majority of profits. We also observed that users were often unaware they were part of a scam until attempting to withdraw funds after the scheme's collapse. Ultimately, this study serves as a cautionary lesson on how such schemes can be engineered using blockchain technology and how users can be effectively deceived. The datasets and simulation tools developed for this research are available on GitHub.

Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models have proven effective in process mining, surpassing traditional methods in predictive performance. Building on this foundation, we evaluate four Graph Neural Network (GNN) variants alongside a dropout-enhanced fully connected Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP) to forecast the next activity's nature and timestamp. Unlike prior studies, we assess these models across various process stages, segmented by quartiles of case duration and activity count. This analysis reveals that model efficacy varies significantly throughout the process lifecycle. Specifically, CNN and LSTM demonstrate superior performance in the process initiation and finalization phases, whereas GNN and MLP models yield better results in the middle segments. Furthermore, we observe that scaling the training dataset by a factor of 10 yields negligible performance gains. These findings suggest that overfitting constrains model potential in datasets with a low volume of logged activities. Consequently, we propose using a robust MLP with dropout as a pragmatic alternative in process mining contexts. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for training deep learning models on business process data. Extensive experiments on multiple common 3D transformations demonstrate that TPC significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art methods; for instance, our framework increases certified accuracy against twisting transformations along the z-axis (within 20°) from 20.3% to 83.8%. The source code and models are accessible at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

This approach successfully located poles corresponding to RPA excited states, including the electric dipole giant resonance in $^{16}$O. While the giant resonance is traditionally characterized as a single state with significant strength and width, the RPA analysis reveals that it actually consists of multiple distinct poles. Each of these poles possesses unique widths, origins, responses to residual interactions, and density fluctuation component structures. The findings indicate that there is not a single "Giant Resonance," but rather a collection of distinct resonances that collectively constitute the giant resonance phenomenon. The pole locations shift individually when the phobic interaction is modified, implying that these states have distinct natures. Furthermore, the RPA calculation demonstrates that pole identification is feasible even with a finite cutoff on the energy denominator. This capability to pinpoint poles using a cutoff-regulated Green's function is valuable for studying the hadron spectrum from QCD theories such as Lattice QCD or Large $N_c$ QCD. This study also highlights that pole extraction via the Jost function method is significantly more efficient than locating poles through standard eigenenergy diagonalization. The proposed technique holds promise for identifying excited states in Lattice QCD and could serve as a novel benchmark for extracting the hadron spectrum from QCD models with energy cutoffs, such as the Dyson-Schwinger equation approach.

In many of these contexts, the underlying systems are dynamic, and due to their inherent complexity, constructing mathematical models suitable for clustering is often unfeasible. Furthermore, effective clustering of dynamic systems must explicitly account for their temporal evolution. This paper introduces a novel methodology for clustering dynamic systems directly from time-series data, inherently capturing the system's dynamical behavior. Specifically, we define a distance or similarity metric between system states based on their mutual influence, utilizing this measure for clustering. To enable data-driven computation, we employ the Koopman operator framework, which accommodates system nonlinearities, thereby extending the approach's applicability to diverse domains. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by clustering three distinct dynamic systems: a linear system serving as a proof of concept, the highly nonlinear IEEE 39-bus transmission network, and dynamic variables derived from atmospheric data across the Amazon rainforest. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of this methodology for other areas of interest.

Drawing inspiration from sparse coding, we introduce SparseGAN, which produces sparse, semantically interpretable sentence representations for the discriminator. Title: Text Generation with Variational Auto-Encoders Compressed by Sparse Coding

Abstract: We present a text generation model where the variational auto-encoder (VAE) is compressed using a sparse coding technique. This approach, termed Variational Sparse Auto-Encoder (VarSparseAE), leverages the fact that many natural images possess low-rank structures to develop a model where the encoder produces a low-rank latent representation. Consequently, the decoder can reconstruct the input image using a few parameters. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the NIST machine translation benchmark and significantly surpasses state-of-the-art models on the WikiText-2 dataset. To evaluate the detectability of this phenomenon, we constructed a mathematical model incorporating key variables such as microbial survival duration, stellar velocity dispersion, and ejecta dispersion. Our analysis indicates that the statistical pair-correlation functions of active stars within the Local Bubble can be explained by an injection event occurring approximately 14.3 parsecs ago, with a 95% confidence interval of ±4.8 parsecs. We further demonstrate that the broader distribution of active stars can be accounted for within a range of 41.3 parsecs (at 95% confidence), a figure that aligns with the radius of the Hydrogen-II region surrounding the Sun, likely generated by the combined radiation of early, massive stars. Adopting the most conservative estimates for life-sustaining ejecta widths and survival times, we conclude that the PAH feature, representing polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, may serve as a potential signature of an ancient supernova remnant from the Cassiopeia A region. By leveraging current and future astrophysical data, we propose that life's presence can be traced via a specific sequence of evidence: life's origin, its injection mechanism, its survival period, and its subsequent distribution. This framework not only aids in interpreting existing data but also guides the design of new observations, potentially enabling researchers to work backwards from the remnants of ejecta to infer the conditions of a system's birth. Ultimately, if life is indeed distributed throughout the interstellar medium, then any star, and by extension any planet, has the potential to harbor living organisms.

A parallel key area in wildlife science involves estimating and modeling population density and size. While recently developed spatial capture-recapture (SCR) models achieve this goal by combining individual encounter histories with auxiliary spatial data on capture locations, they have not yet been extended to explicitly model space usage and resource selection. These SCR models incorporate encounter probability functions that are conceptually similar to RSFs, yet existing frameworks lack the capability for joint inference on these specific ecological processes.

This study introduces a statistical framework for simultaneously modeling space usage, resource selection, and population density. This approach integrates SCR data—such as that from camera traps, mist-nets, or conventional catch-traps—with resource selection data gathered from telemetered individuals. The proposed method relies on marginal likelihood estimation to concurrently determine parameters for both SCR and RSF models.

The results indicate that this integrated method enhances the precision of population density estimates and improves parameter estimation for standard SCR models. Crucially, the findings demonstrate that SCR models alone can estimate RSF parameters, although their performance is superior when combined with telemetry data, especially in scenarios where animals exhibit distinct home ranges relative to the study area's buffer zone. Furthermore, the approach allows for the examination of the drivers behind space usage and resource selection by assessing how environmental covariates influence encounter probabilities.

Overall, this methodology offers a comprehensive approach to studying the spatial ecology of animal populations. By utilizing all available data, researchers can better investigate fundamental ecological questions regarding space usage, resource selection, and population density, ultimately leading to a deeper understanding of how populations distribute themselves across their habitat space.

In this work, we present a method to study Kuramoto oscillators on multilayer networks by utilizing the join of matrices that encode both intra-layer and inter-layer connections. Our geometric theory of testing serves as the specification for a testing environment, which functions as the final stage of a toolchain designed to assist professional developers, hobbyists, and computer science students. This environment features an automated algorithm that identifies errors within executed tests and guides their correction by displaying a stick diagram of causal execution chains on a screen. Users can navigate this diagram backward, similar to using a satnav to follow roads on a map, which highlights the specific locations in the code that require modification to eliminate the error. We have released this environment as a GitHub extension for Visual Studio, which supports debugging, executed test validation, and the entire execution-rejection- correction cycle. The environment is also available for Python on any platform, with source code that can be adapted to support any other language or toolchain. During the Demonstration track of the 35th International Conference on Formal Method Design and Application for Software Engineering (FMODELS), the environment will execute a simple example to reject an execution, followed by a walkthrough of the backward search through the stick diagram to locate the rejection cause. This is contrasted with execution within a standard toolchain, which only indicates an error without specifying its location. Subsequently, the source code of both the test and the example will be embedded using a "reflexive" editing mode, allowing viewers to execute the rejection again and observing how the stick diagram updates in real-time as edits are made. Finally, we will discuss the various types of executions and their interpretations rendered by the environment. The session will conclude with a time permitting Q&A. The soft paper presenting this work can be accessed here: https://www.softpaper.cc/index.php?n=Testing/StickDiagram. The live execution-rejection-correction experience is available at the official GitHub address: https://github.com/zuillgroup/FM2021VSEnvironment.

We operate within the full information model, wherein Byzantine nodes possess complete awareness of the network's state at every step—including all random choices—unlimited computational capabilities, and the freedom to deviate arbitrarily from the protocol. Our primary contribution is a randomized distributed algorithm capable of estimating network size despite a high volume of Byzantine nodes. Specifically, this algorithm accurately estimates the size of sparse, small-world expander networks containing up to $O(n^{1 - \delta})$ Byzantine nodes, where $n$ represents the unknown network size and $\delta$ is any fixed positive constant. The algorithm produces a constant-factor estimate of $\log(n)$ with high probability, ensuring that a large majority ($(1 - \epsilon)$-fraction) of honest nodes obtain the correct network size. Furthermore, the approach is fully distributed, lightweight, and easy to implement; it completes in $O(\log^3{n})$ rounds, utilizes small messages per round, and imposes minimal local computational costs on each node. It is important to note that achieving accurate network size estimation in a fully distributed, sparse, small-world expander environment is notoriously difficult, particularly in the presence of even a single Byzantine node. To our knowledge, this research presents the initial attempt to precisely estimate network size in such environments when a non-negligible fraction of nodes is Byzantine. The algorithm was developed to satisfy the following constraints and assumptions: (i) the network follows a directed random graph model, (ii) the total number of nodes is unknown, (iii) the graph maintains a sparse and highly connected small-world expander property, (iv) the model is full information, (v) Byzantine nodes may act arbitrarily, (vi) the solution is distributed, (vii) the number of communication rounds scales polylogarithmically, and (vii) the message and computation complexities are polynomial. Prior to this study, accurate network size estimation in random graphs with a negligible fraction of Byzantine nodes remained an open problem. Additionally, in the full information model of arbitrary sparse networks, existing solutions either rely on cryptographic primitives or fail to achieve accuracy beyond a factor of two. In contrast, our solution is secure against a large number of Byzantine nodes, operates in a information-theoretic setting, and achieves very efficient execution. In summary, the key outcomes are (A) determining accurate network size estimates and (B) the underlying novel techniques. These findings

This result is attained by analyzing a Plateau-type problem featuring a free boundary, defined both on the obstacle and at infinity, to determine the first obstacle-specific term (termed the {\it isoperimetric residue}) in the energy expansion as $v\to\infty$. These materials possess an inherent self-sensing capability, as their electrical conductivity alters in response to deformation and damage. This phenomenon, termed piezoresistivity, has been widely utilized for damage detection through electrical resistance measurements and tomographic imaging methods like electrical impedance tomography (EIT). While these approaches are highly effective at identifying the existence of damage, they struggle to deliver accurate details regarding the damage's shape, dimensions, or underlying mechanism. To address this limitation, this study introduces a novel technique for precisely determining the shape and size of pressure-induced indentations using a combination of finite element method (FEM) simulations and inverse analysis based on electrical resistance data. The research begins by validating a linearized electrical resistance model with a corresponding FEM model via sensitivity analysis. Subsequently, an optimization problem is formulated to estimate pressure-induced damage using this linearized resistance model. Numerical experiments are conducted to assess the robustness of these methods and the stability of the inverse solution, particularly regarding electrical resistance noise and sensor network configurations. Finally, an experimental validation is performed on a carbon nanotube (CNT)-reinforced polymer specimen to demonstrate the practical application of the proposed approach for accurately detecting pressure-induced indentations in real-world scenarios. The findings indicate that FEM and inverse analysis based on electrical resistance can precisely determine the parameters of pressure-induced indentations. Furthermore, by strategically selecting finite element nodes as sensors and optimizing the inverse analysis, it becomes feasible to resolve complex indentations, such as those caused by inclined pressures, with high accuracy.

While past efforts have predominantly targeted upper limb restoration, the lower limbs have been largely overlooked. Initial feasibility trials employed noninvasive EEG-based BCIs to aid walking in paraplegic individuals, yet the low spatiotemporal resolution of EEG limited these systems to basic gait commands, such as starting or stopping movement. To manage more sophisticated walking patterns, BCIs must precisely decode additional degrees of freedom from neural activity. This study utilized subdurally recorded electrocorticogram (ECoG) signals from healthy participants to create a decoder for predicting walking states and step frequencies. We captured ECoG data from the motor cortices of two subjects walking on a treadmill at varying speeds. Offline analysis revealed that state information could be extracted from over 16 minutes of ECoG data with an exceptional accuracy of 99.8%. Furthermore, applying a Bayesian filter method, we decoded step frequencies with an average error of just 0.3 Hz. When this approach was transferred to data from a paraplegic subject who had undergone an invasive BCI trial, the state decoding accuracy remained high at 98.3%, and the step frequency error was 0.4 Hz. By precisely translating walking dynamics into digital form, this research provides a foundational method for creating BCIs capable of advanced walking recovery. The findings indicate that modern BCIs can robustly decode walking states and step frequencies from ECoG signals in both able-bodied and paraplegic humans. The presented technique represents a substantial advancement over previous decoding efforts, which were confined to simple walking states or failed to match the accuracy, speed, or sensitivity required for practical clinical use. The findings from this and prior related studies form the basis for an hypothesis regarding the location of the neural circuitry responsible for decoding walking states and step frequencies, a hypothesis that can be validated through future decoding experiments in animal models. Clinically, this research paves the way for BCIs that accurately translate human walking into digital formats, enabling the development of advanced gait rehabilitation strategies, such as adaptive assistive devices that respond to the user's intended step rate. An open dataset containing ECoG recordings from two subjects walking on a treadmill is provided to facilitate further research, including the hypothesis that the neural population encoding step frequency operates within a diamond-shaped region of the motor cortex.

While many have developed upright walking to traverse complex terrains efficiently, others, like the fly *Drosophila melanogaster*, utilize a four-legged gait that raises questions about the evolutionary drivers behind motility changes and the trade-offs involved in moving at different speeds and accuracies. By combining motility data from static and moving environments with models of energy expenditure and mechanical work, we investigate the reasons for this shift from non-motile to motile states and the justification for adopting a four-legged strategy over a two-legged one. Furthermore, our analysis of energy cost versus velocity and accuracy reveals that, for a given energy intake, the maximum foraging distance of a two-legged animal is roughly half that of a four-legged one. Consequently, the transition from immobility to motion, and from two to four legs, likely occurs at distinct critical thresholds of foraging distance. These findings are supported by experimental data on *D. melanogaster* and can be empirically tested across various motile species. Overall, this research utilizes a specific animal to explore the questions driving motility evolution and the factors influencing gait selection, while also offering a quantitative framework to study an animal's energy budget relative to foraging distance and accuracy. Motility is essential for organisms to survive, reproduce, and interact within their environments; as they search for food, partners, and predators across rough terrain, efficient motion becomes a primary selective pressure. Although many animals have evolved the energy-efficient bipedal gait, the prevalence of quadrupeds—comprising about 99% of all animal species—warrants a deeper examination of the trade-offs between these two motility strategies. This study focuses on foraging distance as the key driver for an animal's decision to remain stationary or start foraging, and to choose between a quadrupedal and bipedal gait. Using the well-studied *Drosophila* as a case study, we analyze energy costs and mechanical work to explain the transitions between these states. Our results indicate that the states of being stationary, quadrupedal, and bipedal in *D. melanogaster* are defined by distinct critical thresholds of foraging distance. Additionally, our model suggests that a bipedal animal can forage approximately twice as far as a quadrupedal one before depleting its daily energy reserves. Thus, the transition from a four-legged to a two-legged gait in this species may be selected for when foraging distances exceed roughly 1.3 meters

In this study, we investigate a theory in $(2+1)$D defined on an orbital square lattice, featuring two competing dimensions: complex lattice hopping and long-range Hilbert space interactions. These interactions generate short-range Loewdin matrices that determine the many-body eigenstates. By utilizing the many-body slip rule, we identify a topological phase transition marker that corresponds to the anomaly of a two-dimensional U(1) higher-group symmetry, known as the $\mathbb{Z}_2$_2-GAHSS. Additionally, our results indicate that the marking of the doi phase shifts from trivial to $\chi_2$-nontrivial or even $\chi_3$-nontrivial under specific conditions. We also examine the impact of deforming the lattice into a honeycomb structure on these phases and their markings. Finally, we explore the emergence of a quantum anomalous hall effect within the doi phase, along with its dependence on interaction range and strength, as evidenced by the Chern number. These outcomes are based on marking analysis, slip rule-based dynamics simulations, and direct computation of the Chern number.

This paper addresses a distributed memoryless context selection problem where agents observe contexts and select a subset for reporting, aiming to fill a demand distribution with a cost no higher than a given threshold $\epsilon$, despite having access to only $k$ samples from $d$. We introduce a distributed algorithm achieving a communication cost no greater than $\mathcal{O}(k\sqrt{d}+\sqrt{k}\log(d) \log(1/\epsilon))$. This result signifies a progress toward the conjectured lower bound of $\mathcal{O}(k+d)$, which reduces to $\mathcal{O}(k)$ when $d$ is constant. Additionally, we prove a $\Omega(k+d)$ lower bound for the sum of context sizes. For the related problem of sketching a probability distribution, we demonstrate that a context size of $\tilde{\Omega}(k+d)$ is necessary to ensure that the expected size of sampled contexts covers at least a $(1-\epsilon)$ fraction of the total probability mass. Our contributions are distributed as follows: we address a semi-distributed scenario where a central agent interacts with $N$ distributed agents who each observe $k_N$ samples, requiring contexts of size $k$ no larger than $\epsilon$, with $k+N \geq k_0+\epsilon_0 N$ for some constants $k_0,\epsilon_0$. We show that $k \leq \mathcal{O}(k_0+N\epsilon_0/\sqrt{d})$ is achievable. Furthermore, we extend this analysis to a fully distributed setting where agents collaborate without a central coordinator, utilizing a gossip-based protocol where a central agent has access to $N$ samples, resulting in $k \leq \mathcal{O}((k_0+\epsilon_0 N/\sqrt{d})\log(N))$. Finally, we present a reduced model where agents hold samples from two distinct distributions and must report a context representing one of them; we prove that $\epsilon \geq \Omega(1/N)$ is required for a context size no larger than $k$. These findings generalize to the case where agents sample from $M$ different distributions. Our proposed semi-distributed and fully distributed methods rely on Gossip-based Power Iteration and Gossip-based K-Means clustering, respectively. Numerical simulations

By isolating events within the same centrality class but exhibiting significantly varying average flow, we can investigate distinct initial state conditions. Our results indicate that the impact of event-shape selection on the elliptic flow coefficient $v_2$ remains nearly constant across transverse momentum $p_\rm{T}$, which aligns with expectations if the effect stems from fluctuations in the system's initial geometry. Furthermore, transverse momentum distributions for charged hadrons, pions, kaons, and protons show harder spectra in events with above-average elliptic flow, suggesting a coupled interaction between radial and elliptic flow. Finally, the relative yields of hadrons and short-lived hadronic resonances are enhanced in events with elevated elliptic flow, a phenomenon observed in both lead-lead and proton-proton collisions at the same energy, pointing to a possible link with the emergence of a partonic phase. Collectively, these observations reinforce the concept that the initial state of heavy-ion collisions at the LHC exhibits substantial event-by-event fluctuations, and they highlight the necessity of further research into hadronization mechanisms and particle transport within this environment. Although numerical evidence suggests that binary power control is nearly optimal in most practical scenarios, this extremal analysis reveals that significant gains from optimal control can exist in specific settings, while also establishing GDoF-based bounds for these maximum gains. The study's primary contribution is the explicit characterization of the extremal GDoF gain of optimal power control over binary control as $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ for any number of users $K$. Specifically, this gain is bounded between $\lfloor \sqrt{K}\rfloor$ and $2.5\sqrt{K}$. For networks with $K=2,3,4,5,6$ users, the exact extremal gains are determined to be $1, 3/2, 2, 9/4$, and $41/16$, respectively. Networks achieving these extremal gains can be viewed as multi-tier heterogeneous systems. It is important to note that since the focus is on asymptotic analysis, these sharp characterizations of extremal gains hold primarily theoretical value and do not contradict the established understanding that binary power control remains generally close to optimal in practical, non-asymptotic environments. Additionally, the paper provides characterizations of the extremal gain of binary power control relative to optimal control, which is bounded by $\Theta\left(K^{2/3}\right)$; the precise extremal value is identified as $32/9\cdot N^{2/3}$ for networks consisting of $N$ data links and $K=2N$ receivers. Finally, these findings are extended to time division multiple access (TDMA) networks, where the same asymptotic bounds of $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ and $\Theta\left(K^{2/3}\right)$ apply, with the distinct extremal gain of binary control being exactly $N^{2/3}$. All constructions and bounds presented are exact and not merely asymptotic. The network models utilized in this work involve path losses determined by user angles and do not rely on far-field approximations.

Because the time step necessary to resolve collision dynamics is significantly smaller than that required for fluid flow, the computational expense of using the traditional soft-sphere model—which mandates such small steps—becomes prohibitive for simulations involving thousands of particles. While existing state-of-the-art methods artificially stretch the collision time to match several flow solver time steps, this approach introduces non-physical artifacts that compromise simulation results. In contrast, the proposed MTSA employs distinct time steps to independently resolve fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. The algorithm was implemented in the open-source simulation tool Weibo. Both the traditional soft-sphere model and the new MTSA were first validated on a particle approaching a planar wall; the results demonstrated that the MTSA accurately captures collision dynamics with half the computational cost of the soft-sphere model. Subsequently, simulations of particles in planar and planar-plus-pressure-gradient flows showed that the MTSA more accurately captured particle collision behavior. Specifically, while the soft-sphere model exhibited artificial pre-collision deflections and reduced normal velocities, the MTSA produced physically realistic trajectories and collision frequencies. Ultimately, the MTSA offers a low-cost method to resolve particle collisions without introducing physical artifacts, representing an advancement over current state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, the code and library are open source, providing researchers and developers accessing the Weibo simulation code with a superior method for modeling particle collisions. The related library is available at: https://github.com/NCAR/MTSA. The MTSA is expected to be beneficial for any simulation requiring high-resolution particle collisions.

terrain remains a difficult and unresolved challenge in robo-physics, as the uncertainty arising from ground deformation hinders both dynamical modeling and control strategies. Furthermore, determining efficient and stable movement mechanisms on soft ground presents a significant hurdle. This study aims to control a crawling square robot to generate a soft trail that facilitates its locomotion. To achieve this, we developed an optimization framework based on model predictive control (MPC) specifically designed to create a desired soft trail. We validated this approach in both simulation and physical experiments, comparing the results with a baseline controller that executes an optimized gait optimization (MPC-SOTR) to achieve a stable and energy-efficient crawl. The MPC-SOTR controller successfully enabled the robot to maintain a consistent velocity of 1.95 $\pm$ 0.1 cm/s on gelatin with a stiffness of 2.8 kPa, representing a 25% reduction in cost of transport compared to free space. Additionally, the MPC-SOTR controller proactively creates a soft trail matching the target depth profile along the robot's direction of motion, a capability confirmed through high-speed camera analysis. By integrating trail creation and optimized gaits into a unified framework, this research offers a novel solution for organized locomotion on deformable ground. The accompanying code and recordings are publicly available at https://github.com/kyungmin99/soft_trail.

While numerous statistical and computational models exist for automatically generating these hierarchies, current methods often fail to account for the linkages inherent in information networks, which are ubiquitous in real-world contexts. Additionally, existing approaches typically represent topics as abstract probability distributions over words rather than as concrete nodes derived from the original network, and the statistical techniques employed in prior works often lack the capacity to process data at Web-scale. This paper introduces the Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), which leverages a distributed vertex-programming process to compute a nonparametric Bayesian generative model. Experimental results on three medium-sized datasets and the complete Wikipedia dataset demonstrate that HDTM is capable of inferring accurate hierarchies even when applied to large-scale information networks. Although recent studies have examined the impact of misinformation on scientific publishing and information dissemination, there is a lack of research regarding its spread within social media. This study analyzes the propagation of falsehoods compared to truthfulness using a dataset of one million tweets concerning ten current events, evaluated through a misinformation framework. Our findings indicate that rumors and misinformation propagate faster and reach wider audiences than accurate information. Specifically, fraudulent accounts drive this dynamic; when excluded, the speed of dissemination drops by 27% and the breadth by 17%. Furthermore, these accounts predominantly share misinformation (89%), which spreads 27% faster and reaches 17% farther than truthful content. We also observe that event-type and source-language significantly influence the velocity and extent of information spread. Ultimately, we propose countermeasures to mitigate the spread of misinformation, including identifying high-impact rumor propagators, detecting controversial topics, and estimating the ratio of falsehoods within a dataset. HDTM offers a practical approach for assessing misinformation in real-world scenarios. Source code is provided at https://github.com/hy677/hdtm.

Annealing involves slowly varying Hamiltonian parameters to explore equilibrium phases, making it a powerful method for solving complex optimization tasks. Conversely, quenches entail sudden Hamiltonian changes that drive the system into a non-equilibrium state. This study examines the connection between these two approaches, demonstrating that the critical bottleneck of quantum annealing—the minimum of the annealing gap—can be identified through a dynamical quench parameter characterizing the post-quench quantum state. By integrating statistical methods, such as neural network training, with quench data, we can reconstruct the complete functional behavior of the annealing gap. We further show that insights gained regarding the annealing gap, either partially or fully, enable the design of optimized quantum annealing protocols, yielding practical improvements in time-to-solution. These findings are based on simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians, which model challenging instances of the exact cover problem. Our results indicate that for current-state-of-the-art hardware, specific quench signatures are signatures of the annealing gap, a phenomenon observable in experimentally obtained data. Additionally, we outline a protocol to experimentally determine the smallest achieved annealing gap and introduce a novel method to explicitly calculate the time-to-solution. Furthermore, we present a revised protocol that utilizes existing D-Wave processor capabilities to experimentally verify our proposed approach. Ultimately, our strategy for analyzing quenched data and subsequently optimizing quench protocols to overcome the annealing gap offers a practical toolkit for future experimental investigations on actual D-Wave devices.

two-band model for infinite-layered nickelates, derived from $d$ and $s$-like orbitals, can be mapped onto a single-band Hubbard model, identifying the screening of the more itinerant $s$-band as a critical factor. Without screening, a strongly correlated band yields an antiferromagnetic ground state with $S=1/2$ on each site; however, incorporating finite $s$-band screening $U_s \sim 5.0$ ($t_s \sim 1.0$) results in $S=0$ against $S=1$ ordering, indicating paramagnetism. Leveraging simple variational mean-field theory, we compute the full single-particle excitation spectrum, which, despite being approximated, captures the major features of experimental photoemission data. We introduce a simple optimization of model parameters that opens a superconducting gap on the $s$-band, achieved by lowering $t_s$ to $\sim 0.7$t. Although this is a simplistic approach, it supports a mechanism for superconductivity where the strength of the Kondo effect is modulated by spatial fluctuations of the $s$-band charge density. Consequently, these findings suggest that the nickelates can be comprehended within a Frank-Wilson-Kondo framework, provided there are spatial charge density fluctuations arising from a relatively large $t_s$. While this is an approximation, it aligns with the concept of orbital mediation, offering a potential explanation for the unusual properties of these materials, such as their relatively high $T_c \sim 30 K$ and thin finite size layers $L \sim 10 \AA$. Although this is an oversimplified approach, it provides a starting point for investigating the origin of $T_c$ and the single-particle excited state, as well as other phenomena like magnetism and quantum criticality, within a microscopic many-body framework. Consequently, this approach may serve as a useful guide for future material designs, such as inserting intercalants into infinite-layer structures to optimize $T_c$. Although this study focuses on infinite-layer nickelates, the discussed mechanisms and methods are also applicable to other transition metal oxides, including square-lattice copper oxides.

As density rises in compact stars, the sound velocity is anticipated to approach the conformal limit ($c_s/c=1/\sqrt{3}$) at high densities while adhering to the causality constraint ($c_s/c<1$), yet its precise behavior continues to be a subject of intense debate. It has been proposed that the sound velocity serves as a key indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, implying a specific functional form for its density dependence. This study investigates the general characteristics of the sound velocity and adiabatic index across hybrid stars, neutron stars, and quark stars, employing various conditions for the hadron-quark phase transition with differing interface tensions. Our findings indicate that the anticipated sound velocity behavior can also arise from the nonperturbative properties of the quark phase, independent of a deconfinement transition, resulting in more compact stars with comparable masses. Consequently, we introduce a novel class of quark star equations of state that could be validated by future high-precision radius measurements of pulsar-like objects. Specifically, our most massive quark star model reaches 2.4 solar masses with a radius of 19.8 km, exhibiting a surface gravity of $0.54c^2/R$. Furthermore, the phase structure of these quark stars becomes nontrivial above 1.3 solar masses, featuring a first-order deconfinement transition intrinsic to the quark matter. We explicitly formulate the general behavior of the sound velocity and derive the corresponding adiabatic index profiles for these configurations. Our results demonstrate that the sound velocity follows the pattern: it starts at zero, increases to a local maximum, dips to a minimum below the conformal limit, rises to a higher local maximum, and finally approaches the conformal limit as density grows. Additionally, we examine the thermodynamic stability linked to the third family of quark stars and validate our theoretical predictions against existing data on neutron star masses and radii. This includes recent measurements such as the 2.14 solar mass neutron star PSR J2215+2603 with a radius of $19.2^{+2.5}_{-1.8}$ km, the 2.07 solar mass quark star candidate PSR J2215+2603, and the 2.3

formed by superposing squeezed and displaced number states, analyzing their phase space structure with an eye toward Heisenberg-limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Suitable squeezing and displacement parameters are determined such that the state fidelity relative to a metrologically sensitive compass state exceeds 99%. Furthermore, the variance in measurements of small shifts is found to be identical for both the proposed states and the compass states, exhibiting comparable behavior as the average photon number changes.
